notes.front: Crushing chest pain, ST depression in V1–V3 with tall R waves and upright T waves. What should you suspect?
notes.back: Posterior MI (get posterior leads V7–V9)

notes.front: Inferior STEMI (II, III, aVF) plus hypotension and clear lungs; worsens with nitrates. Diagnosis?
notes.back: Right ventricular infarction (preload-dependent; check V4R)

notes.front: Beck's triad (hypotension, muffled heart sounds, JVD) indicates what?
notes.back: Cardiac tamponade

notes.front: A holosystolic murmur that gets louder with inspiration is right-sided; this is called {{c1::Carvallo}} sign (classic for tricuspid regurgitation).
Pulsus paradoxus is defined as what?
notes.back: A drop in systolic BP of more than 10 mmHg on inspiration

notes.front: Kussmaul sign (JVP rises on inspiration) is classic for which condition?
notes.back: Constrictive pericarditis

notes.front: Young athlete collapses during exertion; harsh systolic murmur that gets LOUDER with Valsalva and standing. Diagnosis?
notes.back: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (dynamic LVOT obstruction)

notes.front: Normal QRS duration is less than {{c1::120 ms (3 small boxes)}}.
Murmur: crescendo–decrescendo systolic at right upper sternal border radiating to carotids, pulsus parvus et tardus.
notes.back: Aortic stenosis

notes.front: Murmur: holosystolic, apex, radiates to the axilla.
notes.back: Mitral regurgitation

notes.front: Murmur: opening snap then low-pitched diastolic rumble at the apex; history of rheumatic fever.
notes.back: Mitral stenosis

notes.front: Normal PR interval is {{c1::120–200 ms}}; longer = first-degree AV block.
Murmur: early diastolic decrescendo at left sternal border with wide pulse pressure and bounding pulses.
notes.back: Aortic regurgitation

notes.front: De Musset sign (head bobbing with each heartbeat) suggests what?
notes.back: Aortic regurgitation

notes.front: ECG: short PR interval with a delta wave (slurred QRS upstroke).
notes.back: Wolff–Parkinson–White (accessory pathway)

notes.front: The preferred cardiac biomarker for myocardial injury is {{c1::troponin}}.
notes.back: High-sensitivity assays detect rises within ~1–3 h

notes.front: ECG: constant PR with sudden dropped QRS complexes; often infranodal and may need pacing.
notes.back: Second-degree AV block, Mobitz II

notes.front: ECG: peaked T waves → wide QRS → sine-wave pattern.
notes.back: Hyperkalemia (progressive)

notes.front: ECG: S wave in I, Q wave in III, inverted T in III (S1Q3T3). Classic association? (most common finding is actually sinus tachycardia)
notes.back: Pulmonary embolism (acute right heart strain)

notes.front: High-quality adult CPR: compression rate {{c1::100–120 per minute}}.
ECG: coved ST elevation in V1–V2 with RBBB-like pattern in a patient with family history of sudden death.
notes.back: Brugada syndrome

notes.front: ECG: polymorphic VT with QRS twisting around the baseline, usually with a long QT.
notes.back: Torsades de pointes

notes.front: ECG: deep symmetric T-wave inversions or biphasic T waves in V2–V3 in a pain-free patient = critical proximal LAD stenosis.
notes.back: Wellens syndrome

notes.front: High-quality adult CPR: compression depth at least {{c1::5 cm (2 inches)}}, allowing full recoil.
ACLS: which two cardiac arrest rhythms are shockable?
notes.back: Ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia

notes.front: Name the 5 H's of reversible cardiac arrest causes.
notes.back: Hypovolemia, Hypoxia, Hydrogen ion (acidosis), Hypo/Hyperkalemia, Hypothermia

notes.front: Name the 5 T's of reversible cardiac arrest causes.
notes.back: Tension pneumothorax, Tamponade, Toxins, Thrombosis (pulmonary), Thrombosis (coronary)

notes.front: Without an advanced airway, adult CPR uses a compression:ventilation ratio of {{c1::30:2}}.
Unstable tachycardia with a pulse (hypotension, altered mental status, shock): first-line treatment?
notes.back: Synchronized cardioversion

notes.front: Shock with cold extremities, high SVR, low cardiac output, and HIGH wedge pressure.
notes.back: Cardiogenic shock

notes.front: Spinal cord injury above T6: hypotension WITH bradycardia and warm skin.
notes.back: Neurogenic shock (loss of sympathetic tone)

notes.front: The primary survey in trauma follows {{c1::ABCDE}}: Airway (with c-spine), Breathing, Circulation, Disability, Exposure.
Trauma: tracheal deviation away from the affected side, absent breath sounds, hypotension, JVD. Immediate action?
notes.back: Needle (or finger) decompression of tension pneumothorax — clinical diagnosis, don't wait for X-ray

notes.front: Glasgow Coma Scale: what are the three components and their maximum scores?
notes.back: Eyes 4, Verbal 5, Motor 6 (total 3–15)

notes.front: qSOFA criteria for sepsis risk (score ≥2 = high risk)?
notes.back: Respiratory rate ≥22, altered mentation, systolic BP ≤100 mmHg

notes.front: A GCS of {{c1::8 or less}} is the classic threshold to secure the airway ("8, intubate").
Septic shock definition (Sepsis-3)?
notes.back: Sepsis needing vasopressors to keep MAP ≥65 mmHg AND lactate >2 mmol/L despite adequate fluids

notes.front: Cherry-red skin, headache, confusion in a family in winter; pulse oximetry reads falsely normal. Diagnosis?
notes.back: Carbon monoxide poisoning (check co-oximetry carboxyhemoglobin)

notes.front: Chocolate-brown blood, cyanosis not fixed by oxygen, SpO2 stuck near 85%. Diagnosis?
notes.back: Methemoglobinemia

notes.front: Cushing triad of raised ICP: hypertension (widened pulse pressure), {{c1::bradycardia}}, and irregular respirations.
Bitter almond odor, sudden collapse, lactic acidosis, venous blood appearing bright red (fire victim or industrial exposure).
notes.back: Cyanide poisoning

notes.front: Tinnitus, vomiting, tachypnea; ABG shows respiratory alkalosis AND anion-gap metabolic acidosis.
notes.back: Salicylate (aspirin) toxicity

notes.front: ABG interpretation: what are the normal values of pH, PaCO2, and HCO3−?
notes.back: pH 7.35–7.45, PaCO2 35–45 mmHg, HCO3− 22–26 mEq/L

notes.front: Mean arterial pressure ≈ diastolic + {{c1::1/3 of the pulse pressure}}.
ABG: pH 7.30, PaCO2 30, HCO3− 14.
notes.back: Metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation

notes.front: Causes of a high anion gap metabolic acidosis (MUDPILES)?
notes.back: Methanol, Uremia, DKA, Propylene glycol, Iron/Isoniazid, Lactic acidosis, Ethylene glycol, Salicylates

notes.front: Normal anion gap metabolic acidosis: two classic causes?
notes.back: Diarrhea (GI bicarbonate loss) and renal tubular acidosis

notes.front: Cholinergic toxidrome (organophosphates) mnemonic: {{c1::DUMBELS}} — Diarrhea, Urination, Miosis, Bronchorrhea/Bradycardia, Emesis, Lacrimation, Salivation.
Repeated vomiting causes which acid-base disorder?
notes.back: Hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis

notes.front: ARDS (Berlin): what PaO2/FiO2 ratio defines it (with PEEP ≥5)?
notes.back: ≤300 (mild 200–300, moderate 100–200, severe ≤100), bilateral opacities, not explained by heart failure

notes.front: Pleural effusion: Light's criteria classify it as an exudate if which ratios are exceeded?
notes.back: Pleural/serum protein >0.5, pleural/serum LDH >0.6, or pleural LDH >2/3 upper limit of normal serum LDH

notes.front: Winter's formula: expected PaCO2 in metabolic acidosis = {{c1::1.5 × HCO3− + 8 (± 2)}}.
notes.back: Higher than expected = additional respiratory acidosis

notes.front: Smoker with hyponatremia (SIADH) and a central lung mass.
notes.back: Small cell lung cancer

notes.front: Smoker with hypercalcemia and a central cavitating lung mass.
notes.back: Squamous cell lung carcinoma (PTHrP)

notes.front: Young Black woman with bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, erythema nodosum, elevated ACE, hypercalcemia.
notes.back: Sarcoidosis (noncaseating granulomas)

notes.front: Anion gap = Na⁺ − ({{c1::Cl⁻ + HCO3⁻}}); normal roughly 8–12.
Night sweats, weight loss, hemoptysis, upper-lobe cavitary lesion.
notes.back: Pulmonary tuberculosis

notes.front: Murphy sign (inspiratory arrest on RUQ palpation) suggests what?
notes.back: Acute cholecystitis

notes.front: Cullen sign (periumbilical ecchymosis) and Grey Turner sign (flank ecchymosis) suggest what?
notes.back: Retroperitoneal hemorrhage (e.g., hemorrhagic pancreatitis)

notes.front: A–a gradient: normal roughly {{c1::(age/4) + 4}} mmHg; elevated in V/Q mismatch, shunt, diffusion defects.
notes.back: Normal A–a with hypoxemia = hypoventilation or low inspired O2

notes.front: Charcot triad (fever, jaundice, RUQ pain) indicates what?
notes.back: Ascending cholangitis

notes.front: Courvoisier sign: palpable, nontender gallbladder with painless jaundice suggests what?
notes.back: Malignant obstruction of the distal common bile duct (e.g., pancreatic head cancer)

notes.front: Elderly patient with atrial fibrillation: abdominal pain out of proportion to exam, elevated lactate.
notes.back: Acute mesenteric ischemia (embolic)

notes.front: SAAG (serum–ascites albumin gradient) ≥ {{c1::1.1 g/dL}} indicates portal hypertension.
Severe chest pain after violent vomiting, subcutaneous emphysema, crunching sound with heartbeat (Hamman sign).
notes.back: Boerhaave syndrome (esophageal rupture)

notes.front: Dysphagia to BOTH solids and liquids from the start; barium swallow shows a 'bird's beak'.
notes.back: Achalasia (loss of inhibitory neurons in myenteric plexus)

notes.front: Crohn vs ulcerative colitis: which has skip lesions, transmural inflammation, and noncaseating granulomas?
notes.back: Crohn disease

notes.front: Nephrotic syndrome is defined by proteinuria greater than {{c1::3.5 g/day}} with hypoalbuminemia, edema, and hyperlipidemia.
Chronic diarrhea, bloating, iron-deficiency anemia; anti-tissue transglutaminase IgA positive; itchy vesicular rash on elbows.
notes.back: Celiac disease (rash = dermatitis herpetiformis)

notes.front: Liver enzyme pattern: AST:ALT ratio greater than 2:1.
notes.back: Alcoholic liver disease

notes.front: Liver enzymes in the thousands (ALT/AST >1000): name the 3 classic causes.
notes.back: Acute viral hepatitis, toxin/drug (e.g., acetaminophen), ischemic hepatitis ('shock liver')

notes.front: Normal serum potassium is roughly {{c1::3.5–5.0}} mEq/L.
Hepatitis B serology: HBsAg negative, anti-HBs positive, anti-HBc IgG positive.
notes.back: Resolved infection (natural immunity)

notes.front: Cirrhotic with ascites, fever, abdominal tenderness; ascitic fluid neutrophils ≥250/mm³.
notes.back: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis

notes.front: Bronze skin, diabetes, cirrhosis, arthropathy of 2nd/3rd MCP joints; high ferritin and transferrin saturation.
notes.back: Hereditary hemochromatosis (HFE)

notes.front: Normal serum sodium is roughly {{c1::135–145}} mEq/L.
Teen with liver disease + psychiatric changes + Kayser–Fleischer rings; low ceruloplasmin.
notes.back: Wilson disease (ATP7B, copper accumulation)

notes.front: Prerenal AKI: typical FENa and BUN:Cr ratio?
notes.back: FENa <1%, BUN:Cr >20:1

notes.front: Muddy brown granular casts in urine.
notes.back: Acute tubular necrosis

notes.front: HbA1c of {{c1::6.5% or higher}} meets the diagnostic threshold for diabetes.
notes.back: Prediabetes is 5.7–6.4%

notes.front: Red blood cell casts in urine indicate what?
notes.back: Glomerulonephritis (nephritic syndrome)

notes.front: Child with hematuria, hypertension, edema ~2–3 weeks after strep pharyngitis; low C3.
notes.back: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis

notes.front: Child with massive proteinuria, edema, hypoalbuminemia, hyperlipidemia; normal light microscopy, effaced podocytes on EM.
notes.back: Minimal change disease

notes.front: PT/INR monitors the {{c1::extrinsic}} pathway (factor VII) and warfarin therapy.
notes.back: PTT monitors the intrinsic pathway

notes.front: Hemoptysis + rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis; anti-GBM antibodies with linear IgG staining.
notes.back: Goodpasture (anti-GBM) disease

notes.front: Child with bloody diarrhea then hemolytic anemia (schistocytes), thrombocytopenia, and AKI.
notes.back: Hemolytic uremic syndrome (Shiga toxin, E. coli O157:H7)

notes.front: Crush injury: dark urine, dipstick positive for blood but no RBCs on microscopy, very high CK.
notes.back: Rhabdomyolysis (myoglobinuria)

notes.front: Normal adult resting heart rate is {{c1::60–100}} bpm.
Hyponatremia with euvolemia, inappropriately concentrated urine, high urine sodium.
notes.back: SIADH

notes.front: Hypocalcemia: carpal spasm when a BP cuff is inflated above systolic. Name the sign.
notes.back: Trousseau sign of latent tetany

notes.front: Hyperkalemia with ECG changes: first emergent step to protect the heart?
notes.back: IV calcium (stabilizes the myocardial membrane; doesn't lower potassium)

notes.front: Normal adult respiratory rate is about {{c1::12–20}} breaths per minute.
High calcium with high (or inappropriately normal) PTH.
notes.back: Primary hyperparathyroidism (usually a parathyroid adenoma)

notes.front: Moon face, buffalo hump, purple abdominal striae, proximal weakness, hyperglycemia.
notes.back: Cushing syndrome (hypercortisolism)

notes.front: Fatigue, hyperpigmentation, salt craving, hypotension, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia.
notes.back: Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease)

notes.front: Shock index = heart rate / {{c1::systolic blood pressure}}; >1 suggests significant shock.
Episodic headaches, sweating, palpitations, paroxysmal hypertension; elevated plasma metanephrines.
notes.back: Pheochromocytoma

notes.front: Hypertension + hypokalemia + metabolic alkalosis + low renin, high aldosterone.
notes.back: Primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn syndrome)

notes.front: Elderly type 2 diabetic: extreme hyperglycemia (often >600 mg/dL), very high osmolality, confusion, minimal ketones.
notes.back: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (HHS)

notes.front: Fever in adults is generally a core temperature ≥ {{c1::38.0 °C (100.4 °F)}}.
Fever, agitation, tachycardia/AF, and heart failure in a patient with known hyperthyroidism after surgery or infection.
notes.back: Thyroid storm

notes.front: Galactorrhea, amenorrhea, bitemporal hemianopia.
notes.back: Prolactinoma (pituitary adenoma compressing the optic chiasm)

notes.front: Sudden severe headache, visual loss, and hypotension in a patient with a known pituitary adenoma.
notes.back: Pituitary apoplexy (hemorrhage/infarction)

notes.front: Normal fasting plasma glucose is below {{c1::100 mg/dL}}; ≥126 on two occasions = diabetes.
Microcytic anemia with normal/high ferritin, very low MCV, and increased HbA2 on electrophoresis.
notes.back: Beta-thalassemia minor (trait)

notes.front: Macrocytic anemia + hypersegmented neutrophils + neurologic deficits (posterior columns).
notes.back: Vitamin B12 deficiency

notes.front: Peripheral smear: schistocytes (helmet cells) indicate what?
notes.back: Microangiopathic hemolysis (TTP, HUS, DIC, mechanical valve)

notes.front: On a CBC, a 'left shift' means increased {{c1::band (immature) neutrophils}}, usually from bacterial infection.
Low platelets, prolonged PT and PTT, low fibrinogen, high D-dimer in a septic patient.
notes.back: Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)

notes.front: Platelet count falls by >50% 5–10 days after starting heparin, with new thrombosis.
notes.back: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT)

notes.front: Prolonged bleeding time and mucosal bleeding with a possibly prolonged PTT; most common inherited bleeding disorder.
notes.back: von Willebrand disease

notes.front: Eosinophilia classic causes: {{c1::NAACP}} — Neoplasm, Asthma, Allergy, Chronic adrenal insufficiency, Parasites.
Peripheral smear: Heinz bodies and bite cells after eating fava beans or taking an oxidant drug.
notes.back: G6PD deficiency

notes.front: Sickle cell disease: crampy bone pain is a vaso-occlusive crisis; fever + chest pain + new infiltrate is what?
notes.back: Acute chest syndrome

notes.front: Elderly patient: bone pain, hypercalcemia, renal failure, anemia ('CRAB'); M spike on electrophoresis.
notes.back: Multiple myeloma

notes.front: Corrected calcium = measured Ca + {{c1::0.8 × (4 − albumin)}}.
notes.back: Low albumin falsely lowers total calcium

notes.front: Peripheral smear: Auer rods in blasts.
notes.back: Acute myeloid leukemia (classically APL, M3)

notes.front: Very high WBC with all stages of granulocytes, splenomegaly; BCR-ABL t(9;22).
notes.back: Chronic myeloid leukemia

notes.front: Painless rubbery cervical lymph node in a young adult; Reed–Sternberg cells (owl-eye).
notes.back: Hodgkin lymphoma

notes.front: Serum osmolality ≈ 2×Na + glucose/18 + {{c1::BUN/2.8}}; an elevated osmolal gap suggests toxic alcohols.
Facial swelling, dilated neck/chest veins, dyspnea worse lying down in a lung cancer patient.
notes.back: Superior vena cava syndrome

notes.front: Cancer patient with new back pain worse lying down, then leg weakness and urinary retention.
notes.back: Malignant spinal cord compression (emergency MRI)

notes.front: Expanding red 'bull's-eye' rash after a hike in the Northeast US.
notes.back: Erythema migrans of early Lyme disease (Borrelia burgdorferi)

notes.front: D-dimer is highly {{c1::sensitive}} but not specific: a negative result helps rule out PE/DVT in low-risk patients.
Painless genital ulcer with indurated edges, later a rash on palms and soles.
notes.back: Syphilis (primary chancre, then secondary)

notes.front: High fever for ≥5 days in a young child + conjunctivitis + strawberry tongue + cracked lips + rash + swollen hands/feet. What complication must you screen for?
notes.back: Kawasaki disease → coronary artery aneurysms (echo)

notes.front: Child: cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, then a rash spreading head to toe; blue-white spots on buccal mucosa.
notes.back: Measles (spots = Koplik spots)

notes.front: Lactate > {{c1::2 mmol/L}} is considered elevated; >4 suggests severe hypoperfusion.
Barking cough, inspiratory stridor in a toddler; 'steeple sign' on neck X-ray.
notes.back: Croup (parainfluenza, laryngotracheobronchitis)

notes.front: Toddler, high fever, drooling, tripod position, muffled voice; 'thumbprint sign' on lateral X-ray.
notes.back: Epiglottitis (airway emergency)

notes.front: Cerebrospinal fluid: high opening pressure, high neutrophils, low glucose, high protein.
notes.back: Bacterial meningitis

notes.front: Kussmaul respirations — deep, labored breathing — are compensation for {{c1::metabolic acidosis}} (e.g., DKA).
Fever, confusion, temporal lobe changes on MRI, RBCs in CSF.
notes.back: HSV-1 encephalitis

notes.front: HIV patient with CD4 <200: dry cough, hypoxia worse on exertion, bilateral ground-glass opacities.
notes.back: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia

notes.front: Watery diarrhea after a course of antibiotics in a hospitalized patient.
notes.back: Clostridioides difficile infection

notes.front: Cheyne–Stokes breathing (cyclic crescendo–decrescendo with apneas) is seen in {{c1::heart failure}} and brain injury.
Rapidly spreading painful erythema, pain out of proportion, crepitus, bullae, systemic toxicity.
notes.back: Necrotizing fasciitis (surgical emergency)

notes.front: Hutchinson sign: zoster vesicles on the tip of the nose implies risk of what?
notes.back: Ocular involvement (nasociliary branch of CN V1)

notes.front: Morning stiffness >1 hour, symmetric swelling of MCP/PIP joints, ulnar deviation; anti-CCP positive.
notes.back: Rheumatoid arthritis

notes.front: Virchow's node is an enlarged left {{c1::supraclavicular}} lymph node, classically from gastric cancer.
Joint fluid: rhomboid-shaped, positively birefringent crystals.
notes.back: Pseudogout (calcium pyrophosphate deposition)

notes.front: Hot swollen knee, synovial WBC >50,000 with neutrophils; what must be excluded urgently?
notes.back: Septic arthritis

notes.front: Young man with low back pain improving with exercise, morning stiffness, uveitis; HLA-B27, 'bamboo spine'.
notes.back: Ankylosing spondylitis

notes.front: Sister Mary Joseph nodule is a metastatic nodule at the {{c1::umbilicus}}.
Young woman: malar rash, photosensitivity, arthritis, proteinuria; most specific antibodies?
notes.back: SLE — anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith

notes.front: Older adult with new temporal headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, high ESR.
notes.back: Giant cell (temporal) arteritis — risk of permanent vision loss

notes.front: Proximal muscle weakness + heliotrope rash on eyelids + Gottron papules on knuckles.
notes.back: Dermatomyositis

notes.front: Kehr sign is referred pain to the {{c1::left shoulder}} from splenic rupture/diaphragmatic irritation.
Obese adolescent with hip or knee pain and limp; externally rotated leg.
notes.back: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis

notes.front: Fall on outstretched hand, snuffbox tenderness, normal initial X-ray. Concern?
notes.back: Scaphoid fracture (risk of avascular necrosis)

notes.front: Compartment syndrome: earliest and most sensitive symptom?
notes.back: Pain out of proportion, especially with passive stretch

notes.front: Battle sign ({{c1::mastoid}} bruising) suggests a basilar skull fracture.
notes.back: Raccoon eyes = periorbital bruising, also basilar skull fracture

notes.front: Asymmetric pigmented lesion, irregular border, color variation, diameter >6 mm, evolving. Concern?
notes.back: Melanoma (ABCDE criteria)

notes.front: Flaccid intraepidermal blisters and oral erosions; Nikolsky sign positive.
notes.back: Pemphigus vulgaris (anti-desmoglein)

notes.front: Widespread skin detachment >30% with mucosal involvement after starting a drug (e.g., lamotrigine, sulfonamides).
notes.back: Toxic epidermal necrolysis (SJS <10%)

notes.front: Kernig and Brudzinski signs indicate {{c1::meningeal irritation}}.
High fever, lead-pipe rigidity, autonomic instability, high CK after starting an antipsychotic.
notes.back: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome

notes.front: Hyperthermia, clonus/hyperreflexia, agitation, diarrhea after combining serotonergic drugs.
notes.back: Serotonin syndrome

notes.front: Alcohol withdrawal: visual hallucinations, autonomic instability, confusion starting ~48–96 h after last drink.
notes.back: Delirium tremens

notes.front: Psoas sign (pain on hip extension) suggests a {{c1::retrocecal}} appendix.
Confusion, ophthalmoplegia, ataxia in a malnourished patient.
notes.back: Wernicke encephalopathy (thiamine deficiency) — give thiamine before glucose

notes.front: Teen with low BMI, intense fear of weight gain, amenorrhea, bradycardia, lanugo.
notes.back: Anorexia nervosa

notes.front: Pregnant >20 weeks: new hypertension plus proteinuria or end-organ dysfunction.
notes.back: Preeclampsia

notes.front: Janeway lesions are {{c1::painless}} macules on palms/soles in endocarditis; Osler nodes are painful.
Amenorrhea, lower abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding, positive hCG, empty uterus on ultrasound.
notes.back: Ectopic pregnancy (until proven otherwise)

notes.front: Third trimester: painful vaginal bleeding with a rigid, tender uterus after abdominal trauma.
notes.back: Placental abruption

notes.front: Newborn: bilious vomiting in the first days of life; 'corkscrew' on contrast study.
notes.back: Midgut volvulus (malrotation) — surgical emergency

notes.front: Trousseau syndrome is migratory {{c1::thrombophlebitis}} associated with occult cancer (classically pancreatic).
Infant 3–6 weeks old: projectile non-bilious vomiting, palpable 'olive' in epigastrium.
notes.back: Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis

notes.front: Toddler: colicky abdominal pain, drawing legs up, 'currant jelly' stools, sausage-shaped mass.
notes.back: Intussusception

notes.front: Cyanotic newborn: 'boot-shaped' heart; VSD, overriding aorta, RV outflow obstruction, RV hypertrophy.
notes.back: Tetralogy of Fallot

notes.front: Hypertension in the arms, weak delayed femoral pulses, rib notching on X-ray.
notes.back: Coarctation of the aorta

notes.front: Typical pKa of an aliphatic carboxylic acid, and its charge state at pH 7.4?
notes.back: pKa ~4–5; almost fully ionized (carboxylate anion) at pH 7.4

notes.front: Typical pKa of an aliphatic amine, and its charge state at pH 7.4?
notes.back: pKa ~9–10; mostly protonated (cationic) at pH 7.4

notes.front: Why is an aromatic amine (aniline, pKa ~4.6) far less basic than an aliphatic amine?
notes.back: The nitrogen lone pair is delocalized into the aromatic ring, so it is less available to accept a proton

notes.front: Phenols have a pKa around {{c1::10}}, so they are mostly un-ionized at physiological pH.
Imidazole (as in histidine) has a pKa of about {{c1::7}}, so it is partly protonated at physiological pH.
notes.back: This is why histidine often acts as a proton shuttle in enzyme active sites.

notes.front: Guanidine groups (pKa ~13) are {{c1::essentially always protonated}} at physiological pH.
notes.back: The positive charge is spread over three nitrogens by resonance.

notes.front: Why do quaternary ammonium drugs (e.g. neostigmine) have poor oral absorption and little CNS action?
notes.back: They carry a permanent positive charge regardless of pH, so they cross lipid membranes (gut wall, BBB) poorly

notes.front: Physostigmine vs neostigmine: which crosses the blood–brain barrier, and why?
notes.back: Physostigmine; it is a tertiary amine (can exist un-ionized), whereas neostigmine is a quaternary ammonium

notes.front: H-bond role of a secondary amide (–CO–NH–)?
notes.back: Both: the N–H is a donor, the C=O is an acceptor

notes.front: H-bond role of an ester group?
notes.back: Acceptor only (no N–H or O–H donor)

notes.front: Why are amides much more resistant to hydrolysis than esters?
notes.back: Resonance: the nitrogen lone pair donates into the carbonyl, making the carbonyl carbon less electrophilic

notes.front: Ester vs amide local anesthetics: where is each mainly metabolized?
notes.back: Esters (e.g. procaine): plasma butyrylcholinesterase. Amides (e.g. lidocaine): liver (CYPs)

notes.front: Which metabolite of ester local anesthetics is linked to allergic reactions?
notes.back: para-Aminobenzoic acid (PABA)

notes.front: A carbon–fluorine bond placed at a metabolic 'soft spot' {{c1::blocks oxidative metabolism}} at that position.
notes.back: The C–F bond is very strong and resists CYP hydroxylation.

notes.front: Which functional group lets captopril bind the active site of ACE, and what side effects are classically linked to it?
notes.back: A free sulfhydryl (thiol) that binds the zinc ion; linked to rash and taste disturbance

notes.front: Which functional group in vorinostat chelates the zinc ion of histone deacetylases?
notes.back: A hydroxamic acid (–CO–NH–OH)

notes.front: Ibrutinib's acrylamide group is an example of what kind of warhead?
notes.back: A Michael acceptor (α,β-unsaturated carbonyl) that forms a covalent bond with a cysteine (Cys481) in BTK

notes.front: How does bortezomib's boronic acid inhibit the proteasome?
notes.back: The boron forms a reversible covalent adduct with the N-terminal threonine hydroxyl of the β5 subunit

notes.front: How do saxagliptin and vildagliptin form a reversible covalent bond with DPP-4?
notes.back: Their nitrile reacts with the active-site serine to form an imidate adduct

notes.front: How does a carbamate inhibitor (e.g. rivastigmine) inhibit acetylcholinesterase?
notes.back: It carbamoylates the active-site serine; the carbamoylated enzyme regenerates slowly (pseudo-irreversible)

notes.front: What is 'aging' of organophosphate-inhibited acetylcholinesterase?
notes.back: Loss of an alkyl group from the phosphorylated serine, leaving a stable anionic adduct that oximes can no longer reactivate

notes.front: Which primary functional group do carbonic anhydrase inhibitors like acetazolamide need, and what does it bind?
notes.back: An unsubstituted sulfonamide (–SO2NH2); its deprotonated nitrogen binds the active-site zinc

notes.front: Why are aromatic nitro groups often treated as a structural alert?
notes.back: They can be reduced (via nitroso and hydroxylamine intermediates) to reactive species linked to toxicity and mutagenicity

notes.front: Define a bioisostere.
notes.back: A group that replaces another with similar physical/chemical properties and gives a similar biological effect, often improving PK or stability

notes.front: The {{c1::tetrazole}} ring (pKa ~4.5–4.9) is a classic bioisostere of a carboxylic acid, used in losartan.
notes.back: It keeps the negative charge but is more lipophilic and resists some metabolic pathways.

notes.front: Name a non-tetrazole carboxylic acid bioisostere that is also acidic.
notes.back: Acylsulfonamide (others: hydroxamic acid, oxadiazolone)

notes.front: Why is fluorine such a common replacement for hydrogen?
notes.back: It is small (close to H in size) but blocks metabolic oxidation and changes electronics, pKa and lipophilicity

notes.front: {{c1::Thiophene}} is the classic ring bioisostere of benzene.
Why are 1,2,4- and 1,3,4-oxadiazoles used to replace esters or amides?
notes.back: They mimic the carbonyl geometry and H-bond acceptors but resist hydrolysis by esterases and amidases

notes.front: What saturated cage is used as a non-flat bioisostere of a para-disubstituted benzene ring?
notes.back: Bicyclo[1.1.1]pentane

notes.front: How does deuteration slow the metabolism of deutetrabenazine compared with tetrabenazine?
notes.back: Kinetic isotope effect: C–D bonds on the methoxy groups break more slowly, reducing the rate of CYP2D6 O-demethylation

notes.front: In 5-fluorouracil, what does the fluorine replace, and what is the consequence?
notes.back: It replaces H at C5 of uracil; its metabolite FdUMP traps thymidylate synthase because C5 cannot be methylated

notes.front: Allopurinol is a structural isomer of {{c1::hypoxanthine}} and inhibits xanthine oxidase.
6-Mercaptopurine is a bioisostere of hypoxanthine. What atom swap makes it?
notes.back: Sulfur replaces the oxygen at position 6 (thio analog)

notes.front: What structural feature turns an arylethanolamine into an aryloxypropanolamine β-blocker such as propranolol?
notes.back: An –OCH2– bridge inserted between the aromatic ring and the ethanolamine side chain

notes.front: Which N-substituents favor β-adrenergic over α-adrenergic activity?
notes.back: Bulky groups such as isopropyl or tert-butyl

notes.front: Norepinephrine → epinephrine → isoproterenol: how does growing the N-substituent change receptor selectivity?
notes.back: α activity falls and β activity rises as the N-substituent gets larger (H → methyl → isopropyl)

notes.front: What ring substitution pattern makes β-blockers like atenolol and metoprolol β1-selective?
notes.back: A para-substituent on the aromatic ring (with no meta substituents)

notes.front: Why do catecholamines have poor oral bioavailability?
notes.back: The catechol (3,4-dihydroxy) ring is rapidly methylated by COMT (plus sulfated and MAO-deaminated in the gut and liver)

notes.front: How did albuterol (salbutamol) escape COMT metabolism while keeping β2 activity?
notes.back: The catechol was replaced by a saligenin ring (a 3-hydroxymethyl group in place of the 3-OH)

notes.front: What does an α-methyl group on the side chain of a phenylethylamine (e.g. ephedrine) protect against?
notes.back: Oxidative deamination by MAO, prolonging action and allowing oral use

notes.front: What configuration of the β-hydroxyl gives the active (natural) enantiomer of epinephrine?
notes.back: R (the (−)-isomer)

notes.front: The active enantiomer of aryloxypropanolamine β-blockers is S, yet its 3D shape matches R-epinephrine. Why?
notes.back: The extra –OCH2– oxygen changes the CIP priorities, so the label flips although the spatial arrangement is the same

notes.front: Methylating morphine's phenolic 3-OH gives which drug, and how does it change activity?
notes.back: Codeine; much lower μ affinity, so it acts largely as a prodrug needing CYP2D6 O-demethylation back to morphine

notes.front: Replacing morphine's N-methyl with N-allyl or N-cyclopropylmethyl has what effect?
notes.back: Converts agonist into antagonist (naloxone: N-allyl; naltrexone: N-cyclopropylmethyl)

notes.front: Which opioid receptor residue forms a salt bridge with the protonated amine of morphinans?
notes.back: A conserved aspartate in transmembrane helix 3 (Asp3.32)

notes.front: {{c1::Morphine-6-glucuronide}} is a potent μ agonist; morphine-3-glucuronide has little analgesic activity.
Fentanyl and its relatives share a {{c1::4-anilidopiperidine}} core.
Why does loperamide act on gut opioid receptors with minimal CNS effect at normal use?
notes.back: It is a P-glycoprotein substrate, pumped out of the brain at the BBB

notes.front: State the 'morphine rule' pharmacophore.
notes.back: An aromatic ring attached to a quaternary carbon, which connects via two carbons to a tertiary amine

notes.front: What substituent at position 7 of 1,4-benzodiazepines increases activity?
notes.back: An electron-withdrawing group (e.g. Cl in diazepam, NO2 in clonazepam)

notes.front: A halogen at the {{c1::ortho (2′)}} position of the 5-phenyl ring increases benzodiazepine potency.
notes.back: e.g. lorazepam, clonazepam

notes.front: Why are 3-hydroxy benzodiazepines (lorazepam, oxazepam, temazepam) preferred in liver disease?
notes.back: The 3-OH is directly glucuronidated (phase II), so there is no CYP oxidation and no long-lived active metabolites

notes.front: What does fusing a triazole ring at positions 1,2 do to a benzodiazepine (e.g. triazolam)?
notes.back: Increases potency and makes clearance depend on CYP3A4 oxidation

notes.front: Midazolam is water-soluble in its acidic vial but lipophilic at body pH. Why?
notes.back: At acidic pH its diazepine ring reversibly opens (and the imidazole N is protonated); at physiological pH the ring closes

notes.front: Where on the GABA-A receptor do classical benzodiazepines bind?
notes.back: At the interface between an α subunit (α1, 2, 3 or 5) and the γ2 subunit

notes.front: Why are GABA-A receptors containing α4 or α6 insensitive to diazepam?
notes.back: They have an arginine where α1/2/3/5 have a key histidine at the benzodiazepine site

notes.front: Flumazenil is a competitive {{c1::antagonist}} at the GABA-A benzodiazepine site.
The penicillin nucleus is {{c1::6-aminopenicillanic acid}}: a β-lactam fused to a thiazolidine ring.
What ring is fused to the β-lactam in cephalosporins?
notes.back: A six-membered dihydrothiazine ring (core: 7-aminocephalosporanic acid)

notes.front: Why is the β-lactam of penicillin unusually reactive?
notes.back: Ring strain plus poor amide resonance (the bicyclic system keeps the N non-planar)

notes.front: What do β-lactams covalently modify to kill bacteria?
notes.back: The active-site serine of penicillin-binding proteins (transpeptidases), which they acylate

notes.front: Why is penicillin G acid-labile, and how does penicillin V fix it?
notes.back: The side-chain carbonyl attacks the β-lactam in acid; penicillin V's electron-withdrawing phenoxy group makes that carbonyl less nucleophilic

notes.front: How do methicillin, nafcillin and oxacillin resist staphylococcal penicillinase?
notes.back: Bulky side chains sterically block β-lactamase access to the β-lactam

notes.front: What side-chain group gives ampicillin and amoxicillin a broader Gram-negative spectrum?
notes.back: An α-amino group (more hydrophilic, better passage through porins)

notes.front: Structural difference between amoxicillin and ampicillin, and its effect?
notes.back: Amoxicillin has a para-OH on the phenyl ring; better oral absorption

notes.front: Clavulanic acid differs from penicillins by what atom swap, and how does it act?
notes.back: Oxygen replaces sulfur (a clavam); it is a suicide inhibitor of many β-lactamases

notes.front: Why is imipenem co-administered with cilastatin?
notes.back: Cilastatin inhibits renal dehydropeptidase-I, which would otherwise hydrolyze imipenem

notes.front: Which carbapenem side-chain feature contributes to β-lactamase stability?
notes.back: A trans-oriented hydroxyethyl group at C6

notes.front: Aztreonam is a {{c1::monobactam}}: its β-lactam is not fused to a second ring.
What is avibactam structurally?
notes.back: A non-β-lactam diazabicyclooctane β-lactamase inhibitor that binds by reversible covalent carbamoylation

notes.front: Which bacterial enzyme do sulfonamide antibiotics inhibit, and what substrate do they mimic?
notes.back: Dihydropteroate synthase; they mimic para-aminobenzoic acid (PABA)

notes.front: Antibacterial sulfonamides need a free {{c1::para (N4) amino group}}, or a prodrug that releases one.
Why are N1-heteroaryl sulfonamides (e.g. sulfamethoxazole) more acidic than sulfanilamide?
notes.back: The electron-withdrawing heterocycle stabilizes the sulfonamide anion, lowering the N–H pKa

notes.front: Name four non-antibiotic drug classes that contain a sulfonamide group.
notes.back: Thiazide diuretics, loop diuretics (furosemide), sulfonylureas, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (also celecoxib)

notes.front: What is the parent ring system of steroids?
notes.back: Cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene (rings A, B, C six-membered; D five-membered)

notes.front: Why is ethinylestradiol orally active while estradiol is poorly so?
notes.back: The 17α-ethynyl group blocks oxidation of the 17β-OH and slows first-pass metabolism

notes.front: What does a 9α-fluoro group do to a corticosteroid (e.g. fludrocortisone)?
notes.back: Increases both glucocorticoid and, strongly, mineralocorticoid activity

notes.front: What structural change turns cortisol into prednisolone, and what is the effect?
notes.back: A C1–C2 double bond; increases glucocorticoid relative to mineralocorticoid activity

notes.front: What do the 16-methyl groups of dexamethasone and betamethasone do?
notes.back: Remove mineralocorticoid activity (they also increase glucocorticoid potency)

notes.front: Dexamethasone and betamethasone are {{c1::epimers at C16}} (16α-methyl vs 16β-methyl).
Prednisone and cortisone are 11-keto steroids. How are they activated?
notes.back: Reduction to the 11β-hydroxyl form (prednisolone, cortisol) by 11β-HSD1, mainly in the liver

notes.front: Finasteride belongs to which steroid structural class, and what does it inhibit?
notes.back: A 4-azasteroid; inhibits 5α-reductase

notes.front: Which two fluoroquinolone groups bind (via Mg2+) to the gyrase–DNA complex and are essential for activity?
notes.back: The 3-carboxylic acid and 4-keto group (with the core quinolone ring)

notes.front: The {{c1::6-fluoro}} group of fluoroquinolones greatly boosts gyrase inhibition and cell penetration.
What does a 7-piperazinyl group add to fluoroquinolones like ciprofloxacin?
notes.back: Better Gram-negative (including Pseudomonas) activity

notes.front: Why should fluoroquinolones and tetracyclines not be taken with antacids or iron?
notes.back: They chelate di- and trivalent cations, forming poorly absorbed complexes

notes.front: Tertiary vs secondary amine tricyclic antidepressants: which is more NET-selective?
notes.back: Secondary amines (desipramine, nortriptyline), formed by N-demethylation of the tertiary amines

notes.front: An {{c1::electron-withdrawing}} group (Cl or CF3) at C2 boosts phenothiazine antipsychotic potency.
Phenothiazine antipsychotics need a {{c1::three-carbon}} chain between the ring nitrogen and the side-chain amine.
notes.back: Two carbons gives mainly antihistamine activity (e.g. promethazine).

notes.front: Why is fexofenadine non-sedating, unlike first-generation H1 blockers?
notes.back: It is a zwitterion (carboxylic acid) and a P-gp substrate, so it barely enters the CNS

notes.front: Why was terfenadine withdrawn, and what replaced it?
notes.back: QT prolongation (hERG block) when CYP3A4 was inhibited; replaced by its active metabolite fexofenadine

notes.front: The three parts of a local anesthetic molecule?
notes.back: Lipophilic aromatic ring – ester or amide linker – ionizable (tertiary) amine

notes.front: COX-2 has {{c1::Val523}} where COX-1 has Ile523, opening the side pocket that coxibs fill.
The {{c1::S}}-enantiomer of the profens is the one that inhibits COX.
What natural product inspired captopril?
notes.back: Peptides from the venom of the Brazilian pit viper Bothrops jararaca

notes.front: Why did enalapril replace captopril's thiol with a carboxylate?
notes.back: The carboxylate still binds the zinc but avoids thiol-linked side effects (rash, taste loss)

notes.front: IUPAC definition of a pharmacophore?
notes.back: The ensemble of steric and electronic features needed for optimal interaction with a target to trigger (or block) its response

notes.front: Name five common pharmacophore features.
notes.back: H-bond donor, H-bond acceptor, aromatic ring, hydrophobic group, positive/negative ionizable group

notes.front: General pharmacophore of classical H1 antihistamines?
notes.back: Two aryl groups on a connecting atom X, a short chain (2–3 carbons), and a terminal tertiary amine

notes.front: Which pharmacophore pattern is classically associated with hERG blockade?
notes.back: A basic (protonatable) amine plus lipophilic aromatic groups

notes.front: What is scaffold hopping?
notes.back: Finding a new core scaffold that presents the same pharmacophore, keeping activity while changing properties or IP

notes.front: What does Ing's 'rule of five' for muscarinic agonists say?
notes.back: No more than five atoms between the quaternary nitrogen and the terminal hydrogen for maximal activity

notes.front: Who coined 'privileged structures', and for which scaffold?
notes.back: Evans and colleagues (1988), for the benzodiazepine scaffold

notes.front: Define a prodrug.
notes.back: An inactive (or much less active) compound converted in the body to the active drug

notes.front: Enalapril → enalaprilat: what activates it and why use the ester?
notes.back: Hepatic esterase hydrolysis; the ethyl ester improves oral absorption of the dicarboxylic acid

notes.front: Why is valacyclovir better absorbed than acyclovir?
notes.back: It is the L-valyl ester, taken up by the intestinal peptide transporter PEPT1

notes.front: Which enzyme gives acyclovir its selectivity for infected cells?
notes.back: Viral thymidine kinase (first phosphorylation); host kinases then form the triphosphate

notes.front: How is clopidogrel activated?
notes.back: Two-step CYP oxidation (CYP2C19 is key) to a thiol that forms a disulfide with the P2Y12 receptor

notes.front: Most absorbed clopidogrel is diverted down which inactivating pathway?
notes.back: An inactive carboxylic acid, by carboxylesterase 1 (CES1) hydrolysis

notes.front: Why is prasugrel less affected by CYP2C19 polymorphisms than clopidogrel?
notes.back: It is first hydrolyzed by esterases and then needs only one CYP step (mainly 3A4/2B6)

notes.front: How does levodopa get into the brain, and what converts it to dopamine?
notes.back: Via the large neutral amino acid transporter (LAT1); aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase converts it

notes.front: Why does carbidopa not block levodopa's conversion in the brain?
notes.back: It does not cross the blood–brain barrier, so it inhibits only peripheral decarboxylase

notes.front: How is omeprazole activated?
notes.back: As a weak base it accumulates in the acidic parietal canaliculus, where acid converts it to a sulfenamide that forms disulfides with H+/K+-ATPase cysteines

notes.front: Cyclophosphamide is activated by which enzyme family, to which ultimate alkylator?
notes.back: CYPs (mainly 2B6) to 4-hydroxycyclophosphamide, which breaks down to phosphoramide mustard

notes.front: Which cyclophosphamide metabolite causes hemorrhagic cystitis, and what protects against it?
notes.back: Acrolein; mesna (a thiol that neutralizes it in the bladder)

notes.front: Prontosil, the first sulfa drug, is a prodrug of what, released how?
notes.back: Sulfanilamide, by reductive cleavage of its azo bond

notes.front: Where and how is sulfasalazine activated?
notes.back: In the colon, by bacterial azoreductases, releasing 5-aminosalicylic acid and sulfapyridine

notes.front: What is fosphenytoin and why use it?
notes.back: A water-soluble phosphate ester prodrug of phenytoin, cleaved by phosphatases; easier IV use

notes.front: Why does tenofovir alafenamide cause less kidney and bone toxicity than tenofovir disoproxil?
notes.back: It is stable in plasma and activated inside cells (cathepsin A), giving much lower plasma tenofovir

notes.front: What does the ProTide (phosphoramidate) design of sofosbuvir bypass?
notes.back: The slow first phosphorylation step; the monophosphate is released inside liver cells

notes.front: Lovastatin and simvastatin are given as lactones. What is the active form?
notes.back: The ring-opened β-hydroxy acid (mimics the HMG-CoA intermediate)

notes.front: Azathioprine is converted to which drug, and how?
notes.back: 6-Mercaptopurine, largely non-enzymatically via reaction with glutathione

notes.front: Mycophenolate mofetil is an ester prodrug of {{c1::mycophenolic acid}}.
Which enzyme performs capecitabine's final activation step to 5-FU, and why is that useful?
notes.back: Thymidine phosphorylase, which is more abundant in many tumors

notes.front: Tamoxifen is converted to the potent metabolite endoxifen mainly by {{c1::CYP2D6}}.
Leflunomide is activated by isoxazole ring opening to {{c1::teriflunomide}}.
Methenamine works as a urinary antiseptic by releasing what, under which condition?
notes.back: Formaldehyde, in acidic urine

notes.front: Nitroglycerin is bioactivated to NO mainly by {{c1::mitochondrial aldehyde dehydrogenase (ALDH2)}}.
Minoxidil is activated to {{c1::minoxidil sulfate}} by sulfotransferase.
Dabigatran etexilate and oseltamivir are both activated by what kind of enzyme?
notes.back: Esterases (oseltamivir by hepatic carboxylesterase 1)

notes.front: Why is metronidazole selective for anaerobes?
notes.back: Its nitro group is reduced only in low-redox anaerobic cells, forming reactive radicals that damage DNA

notes.front: Isoniazid is activated by the mycobacterial catalase-peroxidase {{c1::KatG}}.
What is a 'soft drug'? Give an example.
notes.back: A drug designed to be inactivated by a predictable one-step metabolism; e.g. esmolol (ester hydrolyzed by red-cell esterases)

notes.front: Phase I vs phase II metabolism?
notes.back: Phase I adds or unmasks a functional group (oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis); phase II conjugates it with a polar group

notes.front: {{c1::CYP3A4}} metabolizes the largest share of clinically used drugs.
In CYP3A4, '3' is the family, 'A' is the {{c1::subfamily}}, and '4' is the individual isoform.
What do CYP450s need to oxidize a substrate?
notes.back: Heme iron, O2, and electrons from NADPH via cytochrome P450 reductase (they are monooxygenases)

notes.front: Name three CYP2D6 substrates.
notes.back: Codeine, tamoxifen, metoprolol (also many TCAs and dextromethorphan)

notes.front: Which notable property distinguishes CYP2D6 from CYP3A4 regarding drug interactions?
notes.back: CYP2D6 is highly polymorphic but essentially not inducible

notes.front: Name three CYP2C9 substrates.
notes.back: S-warfarin, phenytoin, many NSAIDs (also losartan)

notes.front: Name three CYP2C19 substrates.
notes.back: Clopidogrel, omeprazole and other PPIs, citalopram

notes.front: Cigarette smoke induces {{c1::CYP1A2}}, lowering levels of caffeine, theophylline and clozapine.
Which CYP is the main producer of NAPQI from acetaminophen, and is induced by chronic alcohol?
notes.back: CYP2E1

notes.front: How is NAPQI detoxified, and how does N-acetylcysteine help?
notes.back: Conjugation with glutathione; NAC replenishes glutathione

notes.front: Rifampin induces CYP3A4 by activating the nuclear receptor {{c1::PXR (pregnane X receptor)}}.
How does grapefruit juice raise levels of some oral drugs?
notes.back: Furanocoumarins irreversibly inhibit intestinal CYP3A4, reducing first-pass metabolism

notes.front: How do azole antifungals inhibit CYPs?
notes.back: An azole nitrogen coordinates the heme iron

notes.front: What is mechanism-based (suicide) inhibition?
notes.back: The enzyme turns the inhibitor into a reactive species that inactivates it irreversibly; recovery needs new enzyme synthesis

notes.front: Aromatic hydroxylation by CYPs often proceeds through an {{c1::arene oxide (epoxide)}} intermediate.
notes.back: Epoxide hydrolase or glutathione can detoxify it.

notes.front: What are flavin-containing monooxygenases (FMOs) known for?
notes.back: N- and S-oxidation of soft nucleophiles; unlike CYPs, they are not readily induced or inhibited

notes.front: What does fomepizole inhibit, and why is that useful?
notes.back: Alcohol dehydrogenase; it stops methanol and ethylene glycol from becoming toxic acids

notes.front: Why can succinylcholine cause prolonged paralysis in some people?
notes.back: Genetic butyrylcholinesterase (pseudocholinesterase) deficiency slows its hydrolysis

notes.front: Glucuronidation is performed by {{c1::UGTs}} using the cofactor UDP-glucuronic acid.
Why are people with UGT1A1*28 (Gilbert syndrome) at risk with irinotecan?
notes.back: They glucuronidate its active metabolite SN-38 slowly, causing neutropenia and diarrhea

notes.front: Sulfation by sulfotransferases uses the cofactor {{c1::PAPS}} (3′-phosphoadenosine-5′-phosphosulfate).
Slow NAT2 acetylators are at higher risk of which adverse effects?
notes.back: Isoniazid neuropathy and hepatotoxicity; drug-induced lupus with hydralazine and procainamide

notes.front: TPMT deficiency is dangerous with which drugs?
notes.back: Thiopurines (azathioprine, 6-mercaptopurine): severe myelosuppression

notes.front: {{c1::Dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase (DPD)}} deficiency causes severe 5-FU and capecitabine toxicity.
COMT methylates catechols using the cofactor {{c1::S-adenosylmethionine (SAM)}}.
Which two phase II reactions usually make a drug less (not more) water-soluble?
notes.back: Acetylation and methylation

notes.front: Glutathione conjugates are excreted in urine as what?
notes.back: Mercapturic acids (N-acetylcysteine conjugates)

notes.front: Benzoic acid is conjugated with {{c1::glycine}} to form hippuric acid.
Why can acyl glucuronides of carboxylic acid drugs be toxic?
notes.back: They are reactive esters that can rearrange and covalently acylate proteins

notes.front: What causes gray baby syndrome with chloramphenicol?
notes.back: Immature UGT (glucuronidation) in neonates lets the drug accumulate

notes.front: How does enterohepatic recirculation of glucuronides happen?
notes.back: Biliary glucuronides are hydrolyzed by gut bacterial β-glucuronidase, and the freed drug is reabsorbed

notes.front: How does valproate raise lamotrigine levels?
notes.back: It inhibits lamotrigine's glucuronidation (raising rash risk)

notes.front: What is carbamazepine's autoinduction?
notes.back: It induces CYP3A4, its own main metabolizing enzyme, so its half-life shortens over the first weeks

notes.front: Carbamazepine's active metabolite is {{c1::carbamazepine-10,11-epoxide}}.
Why is aldehyde oxidase a growing headache in drug design?
notes.back: It oxidizes electron-poor aza-heterocycles, is not a CYP (missed by CYP screens), and varies widely between species

notes.front: Morphine is glucuronidated mainly by {{c1::UGT2B7}}.
How do enantiomers differ in properties?
notes.back: Identical in an achiral environment; they differ only in chiral settings (receptors, enzymes, polarized light)

notes.front: The more active enantiomer of a chiral drug is the {{c1::eutomer}}; the less active one is the distomer.
The eudismic ratio is the potency of the {{c1::eutomer divided by that of the distomer}}.
What does Pfeiffer's rule state?
notes.back: The more potent the eutomer, the larger the eudismic ratio

notes.front: What is the Easson–Stedman hypothesis?
notes.back: A chiral drug needs three-point attachment to its receptor for enantiomers to be distinguished

notes.front: What is a chiral switch?
notes.back: Re-developing a racemic drug as its single active enantiomer

notes.front: Single-enantiomer versions of omeprazole and citalopram?
notes.back: Esomeprazole (S) and escitalopram (S)

notes.front: Single-enantiomer versions of cetirizine and albuterol?
notes.back: Levocetirizine (R) and levalbuterol (R)

notes.front: Levofloxacin is the {{c1::S}}-enantiomer of ofloxacin.
Why was levobupivacaine developed?
notes.back: The S-enantiomer of bupivacaine is less cardiotoxic

notes.front: Why would giving pure (R)-thalidomide not prevent teratogenicity?
notes.back: It racemizes in vivo: the acidic H at the stereocenter (α to a carbonyl) exchanges

notes.front: The {{c1::S}}-enantiomer of thalidomide is linked to teratogenicity.
How does R-ibuprofen become active in the body?
notes.back: Unidirectional chiral inversion to S-ibuprofen via an acyl-CoA thioester

notes.front: Does the sign of optical rotation (+/−) predict R/S configuration?
notes.back: No; rotation is measured, R/S comes from CIP rules, and they are unrelated

notes.front: Are quinine and quinidine enantiomers?
notes.back: No; they are diastereomers (they differ at C8 and C9, not at every stereocenter)

notes.front: Labetalol has two stereocenters. Which isomers carry its β- and α1-blockade?
notes.back: (R,R) is the β-blocker; (S,R) is the α1-blocker

notes.front: Which warfarin enantiomer is more potent, and which CYP clears it?
notes.back: S-warfarin, cleared mainly by CYP2C9

notes.front: Most of methadone's μ-opioid activity comes from {{c1::R-methadone (levomethadone)}}.
Why is D-penicillamine used rather than L-penicillamine?
notes.back: L-penicillamine is toxic (antagonizes pyridoxine)

notes.front: Atropine is the racemate of which compound, and which enantiomer is active?
notes.back: Hyoscyamine; the S-(−) enantiomer

notes.front: d-Sotalol vs l-sotalol?
notes.back: Both block K+ channels (class III); only l-sotalol is a significant β-blocker

notes.front: What is atropisomerism?
notes.back: Axial chirality from hindered rotation around a single bond, giving separable stereoisomers

notes.front: Which verapamil enantiomer is more potent, and what happens to it orally?
notes.back: S-verapamil; it undergoes more first-pass metabolism, so after oral use relatively less of it reaches the circulation

notes.front: Lipinski Rule of Five: molecular weight ≤ {{c1::500}} Da.
Lipinski Rule of Five: logP ≤ {{c1::5}}.
Lipinski Rule of Five: no more than {{c1::5}} H-bond donors and no more than 10 H-bond acceptors.
Under Lipinski's rule, {{c1::more than one}} violation predicts poor oral absorption.
Which drugs commonly break Rule of Five yet work orally?
notes.back: Transporter substrates and natural products (e.g. antibiotics, cyclosporine)

notes.front: Veber's rules for good oral bioavailability?
notes.back: ≤10 rotatable bonds and polar surface area ≤140 Å² (or ≤12 total H-bond donors + acceptors)

notes.front: Rough polar surface area ceiling for CNS-penetrant drugs?
notes.back: About 90 Å² (CNS drugs are often lower)

notes.front: Henderson–Hasselbalch for a weak acid: pH = pKa + log({{c1::[A⁻]/[HA]}}).
Henderson–Hasselbalch for a weak base: pH = pKa + log({{c1::[B]/[BH⁺]}}).
When pH equals pKa, a drug is {{c1::50%}} ionized.
An acid with pKa 4.4 is at pH 7.4. What is the ratio of ionized to un-ionized?
notes.back: About 1000 : 1 (each pH unit is a 10-fold change)

notes.front: What is ion trapping?
notes.back: A drug's un-ionized form crosses a membrane and becomes ionized on the other side, where it gets stuck; weak bases collect in acidic compartments

notes.front: Why does alkalinizing urine speed salicylate excretion?
notes.back: Salicylate is a weak acid; higher urine pH ionizes it so it cannot be reabsorbed

notes.front: Why is aspirin mostly absorbed in the small intestine even though it is un-ionized in the stomach?
notes.back: The small intestine has a vastly larger surface area and longer contact time

notes.front: Why do local anesthetics like lidocaine (pKa ~7.9) work poorly in infected tissue?
notes.back: The acidic tissue raises the ionized fraction, so less neutral drug crosses into the nerve

notes.front: Which local anesthetic form crosses the nerve membrane, and which blocks the Na+ channel?
notes.back: The un-ionized form crosses; the protonated form blocks the channel from inside

notes.front: Classify as weak acid or weak base: phenytoin, warfarin, morphine, lidocaine.
notes.back: Weak acids: phenytoin, warfarin. Weak bases: morphine, lidocaine

notes.front: logP vs logD?
notes.back: logP: octanol/water partition of the neutral species. logD: the pH-dependent distribution of all species (neutral + ionized)

notes.front: For a base, logD = logP − log(1 + 10^({{c1::pKa − pH}})).
Problems linked to very high lipophilicity?
notes.back: Poor solubility, faster metabolism, off-target promiscuity and toxicity (e.g. hERG)

notes.front: Lipophilic ligand efficiency (LLE or LipE) = {{c1::pIC50 (or pKi) − logP}}.
Ligand efficiency is binding free energy per {{c1::heavy (non-hydrogen) atom}}.
What does 'escape from flatland' (Fsp3) refer to?
notes.back: A higher fraction of sp3 carbons correlates with better solubility and clinical success

notes.front: Acidic drugs bind mainly albumin; basic drugs bind mainly {{c1::α1-acid glycoprotein}}.
How does adding fluorine near an amine affect permeability?
notes.back: It lowers the amine's pKa, increasing the neutral fraction and improving permeability

notes.front: How does cyclosporine, a large molecule, cross membranes?
notes.back: It forms intramolecular H-bonds that hide its polar groups (chameleonic behavior)

notes.front: What happened with ritonavir in 1998 that made polymorphism famous?
notes.back: A new, much less soluble crystal form (form II) appeared, forcing the capsules off the market and a reformulation

notes.front: BCS class II drugs are defined how, and what limits their absorption?
notes.back: Low solubility, high permeability; absorption is dissolution-limited

notes.front: Fragment 'Rule of Three'?
notes.back: MW < 300, cLogP ≤ 3, ≤ 3 H-bond donors, ≤ 3 acceptors

notes.front: Why are 1,4-dihydropyridines (nifedipine, amlodipine) inactivated by CYP3A4?
notes.back: Oxidation of the dihydropyridine ring to the aromatic pyridine destroys activity

notes.front: Name three drugs built on an arylpiperazine scaffold.
notes.back: Aripiprazole, buspirone, trazodone

notes.front: Serotonin and the triptans share an {{c1::indole}} scaffold.
Chloroquine and quinine are both built on a {{c1::quinoline}} ring.
How do most ATP-competitive kinase inhibitors anchor in the pocket?
notes.back: H-bonds to the hinge region, mimicking adenine of ATP

notes.front: Gefitinib and erlotinib are {{c1::4-anilinoquinazoline}} EGFR inhibitors.
Which key scaffold in imatinib binds the kinase hinge?
notes.back: 2-Phenylaminopyrimidine

notes.front: Which scaffold defines the sartans (losartan, valsartan, irbesartan)?
notes.back: Biphenyl with an acidic group (usually a tetrazole)

notes.front: Imipramine and carbamazepine share a {{c1::dibenzazepine}} tricyclic scaffold.
{{c1::Piperidine}} is the most common nitrogen heterocycle in FDA-approved small-molecule drugs.
notes.back: Pyridine is second.

notes.front: What does a morpholine ring often add to a drug (e.g. gefitinib's side chain)?
notes.back: Water solubility from a weakly basic amine, often with better metabolic stability than a piperidine

notes.front: The thiazolidinedione head group of pioglitazone activates {{c1::PPARγ}}.
Caffeine and theophylline share which scaffold, and what is their main target?
notes.back: Xanthine (methylxanthines); adenosine receptor antagonism (plus weak PDE inhibition)

notes.front: What structurally distinguishes azithromycin from erythromycin?
notes.back: A nitrogen inserted into the 14-membered lactone ring, giving a 15-membered azalide

notes.front: Azole antifungals such as fluconazole inhibit fungal {{c1::CYP51 (lanosterol 14α-demethylase)}}.
Linezolid is the first marketed {{c1::oxazolidinone}} antibiotic.
Hit vs lead vs candidate?
notes.back: Hit: weak activity in a screen. Lead: hit worth optimizing. Candidate: optimized compound chosen for clinical development

notes.front: {{c1::Vemurafenib}} (2011) was the first approved drug to come from fragment-based discovery.
How do HIV protease inhibitors mimic the transition state?
notes.back: A hydroxyethylene/hydroxyethylamine isostere replaces the scissile peptide bond, mimicking the tetrahedral intermediate

notes.front: Osimertinib covalently targets which EGFR residue, and which mutation causes resistance?
notes.back: Cys797; the C797S mutation

notes.front: What is a PROTAC?
notes.back: A bifunctional molecule linking a target ligand to an E3 ligase ligand (e.g. cereblon or VHL), causing target ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation

notes.front: Thalidomide, lenalidomide and pomalidomide bind the E3 ligase substrate receptor {{c1::cereblon (CRBN)}}.
Imatinib is a type II kinase inhibitor. What does that mean?
notes.back: It binds the inactive 'DFG-out' conformation of the kinase (Abl)

notes.front: The BCR-ABL gatekeeper mutation {{c1::T315I}} makes the kinase resistant to imatinib.
What is the 'magic methyl' effect?
notes.back: Adding a single methyl group boosts potency dramatically, often by locking a bioactive conformation or filling a hydrophobic pocket

notes.front: Formula for volume of distribution (Vd)?
notes.back: Vd = amount of drug in the body ÷ plasma drug concentration

notes.front: Formula for clearance (CL)?
notes.back: CL = rate of elimination ÷ plasma drug concentration (also = k × Vd)

notes.front: Half-life: t½ = {{c1::0.693 × Vd / CL}}
notes.back: Bigger Vd or smaller clearance → longer half-life

notes.front: With first-order kinetics, steady state is reached after about {{c1::4–5 half-lives}}.
notes.back: ~94–97% of steady state

notes.front: For a first-order drug, what determines how long it takes to reach steady state?
notes.back: Only the half-life (not the dose rate or dosing interval)

notes.front: Loading dose formula?
notes.back: Loading dose = target Cp × Vd ÷ F (bioavailability)

notes.front: Maintenance dose rate formula?
notes.back: Maintenance rate = target Cp × CL ÷ F

notes.front: Zero-order vs first-order elimination?
notes.back: Zero-order: constant AMOUNT eliminated per unit time. First-order: constant FRACTION eliminated per unit time.

notes.front: Classic drugs with zero-order elimination (at high concentrations): {{c1::phenytoin, ethanol, aspirin}}
notes.back: Elimination enzymes are saturated

notes.front: Therapeutic index (TI) formula?
notes.back: TI = TD50 ÷ ED50 (LD50 ÷ ED50 in animals); higher = safer

notes.front: Potency vs efficacy on a dose–response curve?
notes.back: Potency = EC50 (lower EC50 = more potent, curve shifted left). Efficacy = Emax (maximal effect).

notes.front: Effect of a reversible competitive antagonist on the agonist dose–response curve?
notes.back: Shifts it right (↑EC50, ↓potency); Emax unchanged, surmountable

notes.front: Effect of an irreversible or noncompetitive antagonist on the agonist dose–response curve?
notes.back: Lowers Emax (↓efficacy); not overcome by more agonist

notes.front: What is a partial agonist?
notes.back: Binds the same site as a full agonist but produces a lower maximal effect at full occupancy; can act as an antagonist when a full agonist is present

notes.front: What does an inverse agonist do?
notes.back: Binds the receptor and reduces its constitutive (basal) activity below baseline

notes.front: In a Schild plot (log(DR−1) vs log[antagonist]), a slope of {{c1::1}} indicates simple competitive antagonism.
Definition of pA2?
notes.back: Negative log of the antagonist concentration that requires a doubled agonist concentration (dose ratio = 2) to restore the original response; for a competitive antagonist pA2 = pKB

notes.front: What are 'spare receptors' and their tell-tale sign?
notes.back: Maximal response is reached with only a fraction of receptors occupied; EC50 is lower than Kd

notes.front: Why is nitroglycerin given sublingually?
notes.back: To bypass extensive hepatic first-pass metabolism

notes.front: A weak acid (e.g., aspirin, phenobarbital) is trapped in urine and excreted faster when urine is made {{c1::alkaline}} with sodium bicarbonate.
notes.back: Ionized form can't be reabsorbed

notes.front: In the elderly, {{c1::phase I (CYP oxidation)}} metabolism declines first, while phase II conjugation is relatively preserved.
notes.back: Phase II = glucuronidation, acetylation, sulfation

notes.front: Slow acetylators are at higher risk of drug-induced lupus from which drugs?
notes.back: Hydralazine, procainamide, isoniazid

notes.front: Drugs with a very large Vd (far above total body water) — what does that mean?
notes.back: Extensive tissue sequestration (e.g., amiodarone, chloroquine); little drug remains in plasma

notes.front: Graded vs quantal dose–response curve?
notes.back: Graded: magnitude of effect in one individual vs dose. Quantal: fraction of a population showing an all-or-none effect vs dose.

notes.front: M1, M3, α1, H1 and V1 receptors couple to {{c1::Gq}} → phospholipase C → IP3/DAG → ↑Ca²⁺.
M2, α2 and D2 receptors couple to {{c1::Gi}} → ↓adenylyl cyclase → ↓cAMP.
β1, β2, D1, H2 and V2 receptors couple to {{c1::Gs}} → ↑cAMP.
Which serotonin receptor is a ligand-gated ion channel rather than a GPCR?
notes.back: 5-HT3

notes.front: Receptor type of the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor?
notes.back: Ligand-gated cation channel (Na⁺/K⁺)

notes.front: Mechanism of botulinum toxin?
notes.back: Cleaves SNARE proteins → blocks ACh vesicle release

notes.front: {{c1::Hemicholinium}} blocks the high-affinity choline transporter, the rate-limiting step of ACh synthesis.
Mechanism of reserpine?
notes.back: Blocks VMAT → depletes vesicular catecholamines and serotonin

notes.front: Why is physostigmine (not neostigmine) used for anticholinergic toxicity?
notes.back: Physostigmine is a tertiary amine and crosses the blood–brain barrier; neostigmine is quaternary and does not

notes.front: {{c1::Bethanechol}} is the muscarinic agonist used for postoperative urinary retention.
Muscarinic agonist used for glaucoma and Sjögren dry mouth?
notes.back: Pilocarpine

notes.front: Effect of epinephrine at low vs high concentrations?
notes.back: Low: β effects dominate (β2 vasodilation). High: α1 vasoconstriction dominates.

notes.front: Why does phenylephrine cause bradycardia?
notes.back: Pure α1 vasoconstriction ↑BP → baroreceptor reflex ↑vagal tone

notes.front: Receptor selectivity of dobutamine and its main use?
notes.back: β1 > β2, α; inotrope for cardiogenic shock and pharmacologic stress testing

notes.front: Abruptly stopping clonidine can cause {{c1::rebound hypertension}}.
Classic adverse effect of the first dose of prazosin?
notes.back: Orthostatic hypotension / syncope

notes.front: Before surgery for pheochromocytoma, give the irreversible α-blocker {{c1::phenoxybenzamine}} before any β-blocker.
notes.back: β-blockade first → unopposed α vasoconstriction

notes.front: {{c1::Pindolol and acebutolol}} are β-blockers with intrinsic sympathomimetic activity.
Which β-blockers also block α1 receptors?
notes.back: Labetalol and carvedilol

notes.front: {{c1::Nebivolol}} is a β1-selective blocker that also causes NO-mediated vasodilation.
Succinylcholine phase I (depolarizing) block is {{c1::potentiated}}, not reversed, by acetylcholinesterase inhibitors.
Classic electrolyte danger of succinylcholine (e.g., in burns, crush injury, denervation)?
notes.back: Hyperkalemia

notes.front: Mechanism of sugammadex?
notes.back: Encapsulates (binds) rocuronium/vecuronium, removing them from the NMJ

notes.front: Mechanism of dantrolene in malignant hyperthermia?
notes.back: Blocks the ryanodine receptor (RyR1) → stops Ca²⁺ release from sarcoplasmic reticulum

notes.front: Organophosphate poisoning: why must pralidoxime be given early?
notes.back: It regenerates AChE only before the enzyme–phosphate bond 'ages'

notes.front: Why do ACE inhibitors cause cough and angioedema?
notes.back: ACE also degrades bradykinin → ↑bradykinin

notes.front: Two classic contraindications to ACE inhibitors?
notes.back: Pregnancy (fetal renal toxicity) and bilateral renal artery stenosis

notes.front: {{c1::Aliskiren}} is a direct renin inhibitor.
Mechanism and classic adverse effects of hydralazine?
notes.back: Arteriolar dilator (↑cGMP); reflex tachycardia, fluid retention, drug-induced lupus

notes.front: Mechanism of organic nitrates?
notes.back: Release NO → ↑cGMP in smooth muscle → mainly venodilation → ↓preload

notes.front: Toxicity of prolonged nitroprusside and its treatment?
notes.back: Cyanide toxicity; hydroxocobalamin or sodium thiosulfate

notes.front: Classic adverse effect of dihydropyridine CCBs (e.g., amlodipine)?
notes.back: Peripheral edema (plus flushing, reflex tachycardia)

notes.front: The classic GI adverse effect of verapamil is {{c1::constipation}}.
Mechanism of digoxin's positive inotropy?
notes.back: Inhibits Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase → ↑intracellular Na⁺ → less Ca²⁺ extrusion by NCX → ↑intracellular Ca²⁺

notes.front: {{c1::Hypokalemia}} increases digoxin toxicity because K⁺ normally competes with digoxin for Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase binding.
Classic visual symptom of digoxin toxicity?
notes.back: Yellow-green color vision (xanthopsia) / blurry vision

notes.front: Classic toxicities of amiodarone (organ tests to monitor)?
notes.back: Pulmonary fibrosis, thyroid dysfunction, hepatotoxicity (PFTs, TFTs, LFTs); also corneal deposits and blue-gray skin

notes.front: Why is flecainide contraindicated after MI or with structural heart disease?
notes.back: Proarrhythmic → ↑mortality (CAST trial)

notes.front: Classic risk of class III drugs like sotalol and dofetilide?
notes.back: QT prolongation → torsades de pointes

notes.front: Mechanism of adenosine at the AV node?
notes.back: A1 receptor (Gi) → ↑K⁺ efflux, ↓Ca²⁺ current → hyperpolarization, transient AV block

notes.front: The effect of adenosine is blunted by {{c1::theophylline and caffeine}} and enhanced by dipyridamole.
notes.back: Adenosine receptor antagonists

notes.front: Ivabradine lowers heart rate by blocking {{c1::HCN channels (the funny current, If)}} in the SA node.
Ranolazine inhibits the {{c1::late Na⁺ current}} in cardiac myocytes.
Why must sacubitril/valsartan never be combined with an ACE inhibitor?
notes.back: Neprilysin + ACE inhibition both raise bradykinin → angioedema

notes.front: Mechanism of statins and their classic adverse effect?
notes.back: Inhibit HMG-CoA reductase; myopathy / rhabdomyolysis (and ↑LFTs)

notes.front: Ezetimibe blocks the intestinal cholesterol transporter {{c1::NPC1L1}}.
Mechanism of evolocumab / alirocumab?
notes.back: PCSK9 inhibition → more LDL receptors recycled to the hepatocyte surface → ↓LDL

notes.front: Why does niacin cause flushing, and how is it prevented?
notes.back: Prostaglandin-mediated vasodilation; pretreat with aspirin (NSAID)

notes.front: Fibrates activate {{c1::PPAR-α}}, increasing lipoprotein lipase and lowering triglycerides.
Why does spironolactone cause gynecomastia, and which alternative avoids it?
notes.back: Antiandrogen effect; eplerenone is more selective

notes.front: Loop diuretics inhibit {{c1::NKCC2}} in the thick ascending limb.
Classic loop diuretic toxicity (especially with aminoglycosides)?
notes.back: Ototoxicity

notes.front: Thiazides {{c1::increase}} serum calcium (useful for calcium kidney stones), while loop diuretics decrease it.
{{c1::Ethacrynic acid}} is the loop diuretic without a sulfonamide group.
Acid–base effect of acetazolamide?
notes.back: Hyperchloremic (normal anion gap) metabolic acidosis

notes.front: Neurosurgical/neuro uses of acetazolamide?
notes.back: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (↓CSF production); also altitude sickness and glaucoma

notes.front: {{c1::Mannitol}} is the osmotic diuretic used to lower raised intracranial pressure.
Diuretic used for lithium-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus?
notes.back: Amiloride (blocks ENaC → ↓lithium entry into collecting duct cells)

notes.front: Mechanism and use of tolvaptan?
notes.back: V2 receptor antagonist; hyponatremia from SIADH (avoid overly rapid correction → osmotic demyelination)

notes.front: Benzodiazepines increase the {{c1::frequency}} of GABA-A Cl⁻ channel opening; barbiturates increase the duration.
Risk of flumazenil in a chronic benzodiazepine user?
notes.back: Precipitated withdrawal and seizures

notes.front: Zolpidem preferentially acts at GABA-A receptors containing the {{c1::α1}} subunit (BZ1 site).
Serotonin syndrome vs neuroleptic malignant syndrome: key exam difference?
notes.back: Serotonin syndrome: clonus, hyperreflexia, rapid onset. NMS: lead-pipe rigidity, bradyreflexia, slower onset.

notes.front: Antidote for serotonin syndrome?
notes.back: Cyproheptadine (5-HT2A antagonist), plus supportive care and benzodiazepines

notes.front: Treatment of neuroleptic malignant syndrome?
notes.back: Stop the drug; dantrolene and/or bromocriptine; supportive cooling

notes.front: Why can MAO inhibitors plus aged cheese or cured meats cause a hypertensive crisis?
notes.back: Dietary tyramine isn't broken down by gut MAO → releases stored norepinephrine

notes.front: Treatment of TCA overdose with wide QRS?
notes.back: Sodium bicarbonate (overcomes Na⁺ channel blockade)

notes.front: Classic lithium adverse effects?
notes.back: Tremor, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, hypothyroidism, Ebstein anomaly (in utero)

notes.front: Lithium levels rise with {{c1::thiazides, ACE inhibitors and NSAIDs}}.
notes.back: ↓renal lithium clearance

notes.front: Major toxicities of valproate?
notes.back: Hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis, neural tube defects; weight gain, tremor

notes.front: Major adverse effects of carbamazepine?
notes.back: Agranulocytosis/aplastic anemia, SIADH, SJS/TEN, teratogenicity; induces CYP3A4 (autoinduction)

notes.front: Screen for {{c1::HLA-B*15:02}} before carbamazepine in patients of East/Southeast Asian ancestry (SJS/TEN risk).
Classic chronic adverse effects of phenytoin?
notes.back: Gingival hyperplasia, hirsutism, nystagmus/ataxia, peripheral neuropathy, teratogenicity

notes.front: Mechanism of ethosuximide and its indication?
notes.back: Blocks thalamic T-type Ca²⁺ channels; absence seizures

notes.front: Levetiracetam binds the synaptic vesicle protein {{c1::SV2A}}.
Classic adverse effects of topiramate?
notes.back: Kidney stones, weight loss, cognitive slowing/word-finding trouble, angle-closure glaucoma

notes.front: Why must lamotrigine be titrated slowly?
notes.back: Risk of SJS/TEN (higher with valproate coadministration)

notes.front: Order in which antipsychotic extrapyramidal effects appear?
notes.back: Acute dystonia (hours–days) → akathisia → parkinsonism (weeks) → tardive dyskinesia (months–years)

notes.front: Drug class used to treat tardive dyskinesia?
notes.back: VMAT2 inhibitors (valbenazine, deutetrabenazine)

notes.front: Clozapine: indication and must-monitor toxicity?
notes.back: Treatment-resistant schizophrenia (↓suicidality); agranulocytosis → monitor ANC; also myocarditis and seizures

notes.front: Why is carbidopa combined with levodopa?
notes.back: Inhibits peripheral DOPA decarboxylase → more levodopa reaches the brain, fewer peripheral side effects

notes.front: Peripheral COMT inhibitor used in Parkinson disease?
notes.back: Entacapone (tolcapone is central and hepatotoxic)

notes.front: Opioid receptor signaling at the synapse?
notes.back: μ (Gi): presynaptic ↓Ca²⁺ influx (less transmitter release), postsynaptic ↑K⁺ efflux (hyperpolarization)

notes.front: Tolerance does not develop to opioid-induced {{c1::miosis and constipation}}.
Mechanism of triptans and a key contraindication?
notes.back: 5-HT1B/1D agonists; contraindicated in coronary artery disease / Prinzmetal angina (vasoconstriction)

notes.front: Mechanism of memantine?
notes.back: NMDA receptor antagonist (blocks excitotoxicity)

notes.front: Bupropion: mechanism and key contraindication?
notes.back: NE/DA reuptake inhibitor; lowers seizure threshold → avoid in seizure disorders and bulimia/anorexia

notes.front: Mechanism of mirtazapine?
notes.back: α2 antagonist (↑NE and 5-HT release); also 5-HT2/5-HT3 and H1 blockade → sedation, weight gain

notes.front: The classic serious adverse effect of trazodone is {{c1::priapism}}.
Inhaled anesthetics with low blood:gas solubility have {{c1::faster}} induction and recovery.
Relationship between MAC and anesthetic potency?
notes.back: Inversely related: lower MAC = more potent

notes.front: Why are local anesthetics less effective in infected tissue?
notes.back: Acidic pH → more drug ionized → less crosses the nerve membrane (uncharged form crosses; charged form blocks the Na⁺ channel from inside)

notes.front: Bupivacaine cardiotoxicity is treated with {{c1::IV lipid emulsion}}.
Mechanism of β-lactams?
notes.back: Bind penicillin-binding proteins (transpeptidases) → block peptidoglycan cross-linking

notes.front: Mechanism of MRSA's β-lactam resistance?
notes.back: mecA gene → altered PBP2a with low β-lactam affinity

notes.front: Ceftaroline is a {{c1::5th}}-generation cephalosporin, the only generation with MRSA activity.
Mechanism of vancomycin, and how enterococci resist it?
notes.back: Binds D-Ala-D-Ala of cell-wall precursors; resistance by D-Ala-D-Lac substitution

notes.front: Cause and prevention of vancomycin flushing ('red man') reaction?
notes.back: Non-IgE histamine release; slow the infusion, antihistamine pretreatment

notes.front: Why don't aminoglycosides work against anaerobes?
notes.back: Uptake into bacteria requires oxygen-dependent transport

notes.front: Main toxicities of aminoglycosides?
notes.back: Nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity, neuromuscular blockade; teratogenic

notes.front: Why shouldn't tetracyclines be taken with milk or antacids?
notes.back: Divalent/trivalent cations (Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺, Fe²⁺, Al³⁺) chelate them → ↓absorption

notes.front: Erythromycin is a {{c1::motilin receptor agonist}}, so it is sometimes used for gastroparesis.
Gray baby syndrome is caused by which antibiotic, and why?
notes.back: Chloramphenicol; neonates lack enough UDP-glucuronosyltransferase

notes.front: Linezolid: two classic adverse effects?
notes.back: Myelosuppression (especially thrombocytopenia) and serotonin syndrome (weak MAO inhibition); also optic/peripheral neuropathy

notes.front: Mechanism of fluoroquinolones?
notes.back: Inhibit DNA gyrase (topoisomerase II) and topoisomerase IV

notes.front: Classic musculoskeletal risk of fluoroquinolones?
notes.back: Tendinopathy/Achilles tendon rupture (higher in elderly and with corticosteroids)

notes.front: Why does trimethoprim cause hyperkalemia?
notes.back: Blocks ENaC in the collecting duct (amiloride-like)

notes.front: Why are sulfonamides avoided in neonates?
notes.back: Displace bilirubin from albumin → kernicterus

notes.front: Reaction when metronidazole is combined with alcohol?
notes.back: Disulfiram-like reaction (flushing, nausea, tachycardia)

notes.front: Mechanism of rifampin and its harmless but classic side effect?
notes.back: Inhibits bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase; red-orange body fluids

notes.front: Isoniazid: activation enzyme and why pyridoxine is co-given?
notes.back: Activated by bacterial KatG; pyridoxine (B6) prevents peripheral neuropathy

notes.front: Ethambutol classically causes {{c1::optic neuritis}} (↓acuity, red–green color blindness).
Why is imipenem given with cilastatin?
notes.back: Cilastatin inhibits renal dehydropeptidase I, which inactivates imipenem

notes.front: Why is aztreonam useful in penicillin allergy?
notes.back: Monobactam with essentially no cross-reactivity with penicillins (gram-negative coverage only)

notes.front: Daptomycin is not used for pneumonia because it is inactivated by {{c1::pulmonary surfactant}}.
Mechanism and major toxicity of amphotericin B?
