notes.back: Binds ergosterol → membrane pores; nephrotoxicity (with hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia) and infusion reactions

notes.front: Azole antifungals inhibit {{c1::lanosterol 14α-demethylase}} (fungal CYP51), blocking ergosterol synthesis.
Mechanism of echinocandins (e.g., caspofungin)?
notes.back: Inhibit β-(1,3)-D-glucan synthesis in the fungal cell wall

notes.front: Terbinafine inhibits {{c1::squalene epoxidase}}.
Acyclovir activation and resistance?
notes.back: First phosphorylated by viral thymidine kinase; resistance via mutated/absent viral TK

notes.front: Why does foscarnet work against TK-deficient HSV?
notes.back: Pyrophosphate analog that inhibits viral DNA polymerase directly — no activation by viral kinase needed

notes.front: Classic electrolyte toxicity of foscarnet?
notes.back: Hypocalcemia and hypomagnesemia (chelation), plus nephrotoxicity

notes.front: Mechanism of oseltamivir?
notes.back: Neuraminidase inhibitor → blocks release of new influenza virions

notes.front: Test for {{c1::HLA-B*57:01}} before starting abacavir (hypersensitivity risk).
Mechanism of maraviroc?
notes.back: CCR5 co-receptor antagonist (blocks HIV entry)

notes.front: Name four β-lactamase inhibitors.
notes.back: Clavulanate, sulbactam, tazobactam, avibactam

notes.front: Methotrexate: target and rescue agent?
notes.back: Inhibits dihydrofolate reductase; leucovorin (folinic acid) rescue

notes.front: Leucovorin {{c1::enhances}} 5-FU activity by stabilizing the 5-FdUMP–thymidylate synthase complex.
notes.back: Opposite of its rescue role with methotrexate

notes.front: Cyclophosphamide: cause of hemorrhagic cystitis and its prevention?
notes.back: Acrolein metabolite; mesna (plus hydration)

notes.front: Main toxicities of cisplatin?
notes.back: Nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity, peripheral neuropathy, severe nausea

notes.front: Doxorubicin: classic toxicity and cardioprotective agent?
notes.back: Dilated cardiomyopathy (cumulative); dexrazoxane

notes.front: The classic toxicity of bleomycin is {{c1::pulmonary fibrosis}}.
Vincristine binds tubulin and {{c1::prevents microtubule polymerization}}; paclitaxel instead stabilizes microtubules.
The dose-limiting toxicity of vincristine is {{c1::peripheral neuropathy}}.
Topoisomerase targets of etoposide vs irinotecan?
notes.back: Etoposide: topoisomerase II. Irinotecan/topotecan: topoisomerase I.

notes.front: Imatinib targets?
notes.back: BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase (CML) and c-KIT (GIST)

notes.front: Trastuzumab's cardiotoxicity vs anthracyclines?
notes.back: Trastuzumab: usually reversible. Anthracyclines: dose-dependent, often irreversible.

notes.front: Tamoxifen vs raloxifene at the endometrium?
notes.back: Tamoxifen is a partial agonist there (↑endometrial cancer risk); raloxifene is an antagonist

notes.front: Why must azathioprine/6-mercaptopurine doses be cut with allopurinol?
notes.back: Allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase, which inactivates 6-MP → toxicity

notes.front: Mechanism of pembrolizumab/nivolumab and their typical toxicity class?
notes.back: PD-1 checkpoint inhibitors; immune-related adverse events (colitis, hepatitis, thyroiditis, pneumonitis)

notes.front: Hydroxyurea: target and use in sickle cell disease?
notes.back: Inhibits ribonucleotide reductase; ↑fetal hemoglobin (HbF)

notes.front: Why is rasburicase contraindicated in G6PD deficiency?
notes.back: It generates H2O2 while degrading uric acid → hemolysis (and methemoglobinemia)

notes.front: Alkylating agent used for glioblastoma, and the biomarker predicting response?
notes.back: Temozolomide; MGMT promoter methylation predicts better response

notes.front: Bevacizumab: target and classic adverse effects?
notes.back: VEGF-A; impaired wound healing, bleeding, GI perforation, hypertension

notes.front: Metformin: main mechanism and rare serious adverse effect?
notes.back: ↓hepatic gluconeogenesis (AMPK activation); lactic acidosis (risk ↑ with renal failure)

notes.front: Mechanism of sulfonylureas?
notes.back: Close β-cell K-ATP channels → depolarization → Ca²⁺ influx → insulin release

notes.front: Classic adverse effects of SGLT2 inhibitors?
notes.back: Genital mycotic infections/UTIs, euglycemic DKA, volume depletion

notes.front: Contraindication to GLP-1 agonists?
notes.back: Personal/family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or MEN2

notes.front: Thiazolidinediones: receptor and key contraindication?
notes.back: PPAR-γ agonists; heart failure (fluid retention)

notes.front: Insulin treats acute hyperkalemia by {{c1::shifting K⁺ into cells}} (via Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase).
notes.back: Give with glucose

notes.front: Why is PTU preferred over methimazole in the first trimester?
notes.back: Methimazole is teratogenic (aplasia cutis); PTU is used early, then switched due to its hepatotoxicity

notes.front: Extra action of PTU that methimazole lacks?
notes.back: Inhibits peripheral deiodination of T4 → T3

notes.front: How do glucocorticoids block arachidonic acid release?
notes.back: Induce annexin A1 (lipocortin) → inhibits phospholipase A2

notes.front: Bisphosphonates: mechanism and why patients stay upright after taking them?
notes.back: Pyrophosphate analogs that inhibit osteoclasts; prevents pill esophagitis

notes.front: Teriparatide (PTH analog) builds bone only when given {{c1::intermittently}}; continuous PTH causes resorption.
Denosumab is a monoclonal antibody against {{c1::RANKL}}.
Leuprolide given {{c1::continuously}} suppresses LH/FSH (after an initial flare); pulsatile GnRH stimulates them.
Uses of octreotide?
notes.back: Acromegaly, carcinoid syndrome, VIPoma, variceal bleeding, sulfonylurea overdose

notes.front: First-line drug class for prolactinoma?
notes.back: Dopamine D2 agonists (cabergoline, bromocriptine)

notes.front: Mechanism of cinacalcet?
notes.back: Calcimimetic: sensitizes the calcium-sensing receptor on parathyroid cells → ↓PTH

notes.front: Finasteride inhibits {{c1::5α-reductase}}, lowering DHT.
Mechanism of PPIs and three long-term risks?
notes.back: Irreversibly inhibit parietal-cell H⁺/K⁺-ATPase; C. difficile, hypomagnesemia, fractures (also B12 deficiency)

notes.front: Two unique problems with cimetidine among H2 blockers?
notes.back: CYP450 inhibition and antiandrogenic effects (gynecomastia)

notes.front: Misoprostol: mechanism, use, and contraindication?
notes.back: PGE1 analog; prevents NSAID ulcers; contraindicated in pregnancy (abortifacient)

notes.front: Mechanism and notable risks of ondansetron?
notes.back: 5-HT3 antagonist; QT prolongation, constipation, headache

notes.front: Metoclopramide: mechanism and serious neuro adverse effect?
notes.back: D2 antagonist (prokinetic); tardive dyskinesia / EPS

notes.front: Why does sucralfate interact with PPIs?
notes.back: It needs an acidic environment to polymerize and coat ulcers

notes.front: Aprepitant is an antiemetic that blocks the {{c1::NK1 (substance P)}} receptor.
Required screening before starting infliximab or other TNF-α inhibitors?
notes.back: Latent tuberculosis

notes.front: How does lactulose treat hepatic encephalopathy?
notes.back: Colonic bacteria acidify it → NH3 trapped as NH4⁺ and excreted

notes.front: Why does loperamide lack central opioid effects?
notes.back: Poor BBB penetration (P-glycoprotein efflux)

notes.front: Mechanism of unfractionated heparin?
notes.back: Activates antithrombin → inhibits thrombin (IIa) and factor Xa

notes.front: Unfractionated heparin is monitored with {{c1::aPTT}}; warfarin with PT/INR.
Reversal agent for heparin?
notes.back: Protamine sulfate (only partial for LMWH)

notes.front: Pathophysiology and treatment of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT)?
notes.back: IgG against heparin–PF4 complexes → platelet activation, thrombosis; stop heparin, give a non-heparin anticoagulant (e.g., argatroban)

notes.front: Warfarin's molecular target?
notes.back: Vitamin K epoxide reductase (VKORC1) → ↓γ-carboxylation of II, VII, IX, X, protein C and S

notes.front: The PT/INR rises first on warfarin because factor {{c1::VII}} has the shortest half-life.
Cause of warfarin-induced skin necrosis?
notes.back: Protein C (short half-life) drops first → transient hypercoagulable state; prevented by heparin bridging

notes.front: Urgent reversal of warfarin with major bleeding?
notes.back: 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate + IV vitamin K

notes.front: Dabigatran is reversed by {{c1::idarucizumab}}.
Apixaban and rivaroxaban are reversed by {{c1::andexanet alfa}}.
Mechanism of aspirin on platelets?
notes.back: Irreversibly acetylates COX-1 (and COX-2) → ↓thromboxane A2 for the platelet's lifespan

notes.front: Clopidogrel is a prodrug activated by {{c1::CYP2C19}}; poor metabolizers get less antiplatelet effect.
How does ticagrelor differ from clopidogrel?
notes.back: Reversible P2Y12 blocker, not a prodrug; can cause dyspnea

notes.front: Target of abciximab, eptifibatide and tirofiban?
notes.back: Platelet glycoprotein IIb/IIIa (blocks fibrinogen binding)

notes.front: Antifibrinolytic agents used to reverse thrombolytics like alteplase?
notes.back: Aminocaproic acid or tranexamic acid

notes.front: Cilostazol: mechanism, use and contraindication?
notes.back: PDE3 inhibitor; intermittent claudication; contraindicated in heart failure

notes.front: Why does fondaparinux rarely cause HIT?
notes.back: It's a synthetic pentasaccharide too short to form the heparin–PF4 complex

notes.front: Toxic metabolite in acetaminophen overdose and the antidote?
notes.back: NAPQI; N-acetylcysteine (replenishes glutathione)

notes.front: Antidote for methanol or ethylene glycol poisoning and its mechanism?
notes.back: Fomepizole — inhibits alcohol dehydrogenase

notes.front: Ethylene glycol poisoning produces {{c1::calcium oxalate}} crystals in urine and acute kidney injury.
notes.back: Methanol → formic acid → vision loss

notes.front: Antidote for cyanide poisoning?
notes.back: Hydroxocobalamin (alternatives: nitrites + sodium thiosulfate)

notes.front: Antidote for methemoglobinemia, and when it's contraindicated?
notes.back: Methylene blue; G6PD deficiency (ineffective, causes hemolysis)

notes.front: Drugs classically causing methemoglobinemia?
notes.back: Dapsone, benzocaine and other local anesthetics, nitrites/nitrates

notes.front: Chelators for lead poisoning?
notes.back: Succimer (mild, oral); dimercaprol + CaNa2-EDTA for severe/encephalopathy

notes.front: The antidote for iron overdose is {{c1::deferoxamine}}.
Acid–base pattern of salicylate toxicity?
notes.back: Early respiratory alkalosis + anion-gap metabolic acidosis (mixed)

notes.front: Antidote for β-blocker overdose and why it works?
notes.back: Glucagon — raises cAMP independent of β-receptors

notes.front: Torsades de pointes is treated with {{c1::IV magnesium sulfate}}.
Isoniazid overdose seizures are treated with {{c1::pyridoxine (vitamin B6)}}.
Antidote for digoxin toxicity?
notes.back: Digoxin immune Fab

notes.front: Antidote for opioid overdose?
notes.back: Naloxone (competitive μ antagonist)

notes.front: Two antidotes used for an organophosphate exposure?
notes.back: Atropine (muscarinic block) + pralidoxime (AChE reactivation)

notes.front: Classic CYP450 inducers?
notes.back: Rifampin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital, St. John's wort, griseofulvin, chronic alcohol

notes.front: Classic CYP3A4 inhibitors?
notes.back: Grapefruit juice, azoles (ketoconazole), macrolides (clarithromycin), ritonavir, amiodarone

notes.front: Why is low-dose ritonavir added to other HIV protease inhibitors?
notes.back: Strong CYP3A4 inhibition 'boosts' their levels

notes.front: Why are CYP2D6 ultrarapid metabolizers at risk with codeine?
notes.back: Codeine → morphine conversion is faster → opioid toxicity

notes.front: Why avoid paroxetine/fluoxetine with tamoxifen?
notes.back: They inhibit CYP2D6 → ↓conversion of tamoxifen to active endoxifen

notes.front: Why do clarithromycin + simvastatin raise rhabdomyolysis risk?
notes.back: Clarithromycin inhibits CYP3A4 → ↑statin levels

notes.front: Why do TMP-SMX, metronidazole and fluconazole raise the INR on warfarin?
notes.back: Inhibit CYP2C9, which metabolizes S-warfarin

notes.front: Why can rifampin cause oral contraceptive failure?
notes.back: CYP3A4 induction → ↓estrogen/progestin levels

notes.front: The 'triple whammy' for acute kidney injury?
notes.back: NSAID + ACE inhibitor/ARB + diuretic

notes.front: Why can MAOIs + meperidine, tramadol or dextromethorphan be dangerous?
notes.back: Serotonin syndrome

notes.front: Cyclosporine vs tacrolimus binding proteins?
notes.back: Cyclosporine binds cyclophilin; tacrolimus binds FKBP12 — both inhibit calcineurin

notes.front: Main toxicity shared by calcineurin inhibitors that sirolimus lacks?
notes.back: Nephrotoxicity (sirolimus inhibits mTOR instead)

notes.front: Mycophenolate inhibits {{c1::IMP dehydrogenase}}, reducing guanine synthesis in lymphocytes.
Why is a LABA (e.g., salmeterol) never used alone in asthma?
notes.back: LABA monotherapy ↑risk of severe/fatal exacerbations; always pair with an inhaled corticosteroid

notes.front: Montelukast vs zileuton mechanism?
notes.back: Montelukast: CysLT1 receptor antagonist. Zileuton: 5-lipoxygenase inhibitor.

notes.front: Why does theophylline need level monitoring?
notes.back: Narrow therapeutic index (seizures, arrhythmias); CYP1A2 substrate

notes.front: Mechanism of colchicine in gout?
notes.back: Binds tubulin → inhibits microtubule polymerization → ↓neutrophil migration

notes.front: Allopurinol vs probenecid mechanism?
notes.back: Allopurinol: xanthine oxidase inhibitor (↓uric acid production). Probenecid: ↓renal uric acid reabsorption.

notes.front: NSAIDs reduce GFR by constricting the {{c1::afferent}} arteriole (↓prostaglandins); ACE inhibitors dilate the efferent arteriole.
Why can sildenafil cause blue-tinged vision?
notes.back: Cross-inhibits retinal PDE6

notes.front: Classic cosmetic side effect of latanoprost eye drops?
notes.back: Darkening of the iris (and eyelash growth)

notes.front: Where do first-order DCML neurons synapse?
notes.back: Nucleus gracilis and nucleus cuneatus in the caudal medulla

notes.front: Where does the spinothalamic tract decussate?
notes.back: Anterior white commissure of the spinal cord, within 1–2 segments of entry

notes.front: Which modalities does the lateral spinothalamic tract carry?
notes.back: Pain and temperature

notes.front: Where does the lateral corticospinal tract decussate?
notes.back: Pyramidal decussation, caudal medulla (~85–90% of fibers cross)

notes.front: Which part of the internal capsule carries corticospinal fibers?
notes.back: Posterior limb

notes.front: Dorsal spinocerebellar tract: origin and peduncle?
notes.back: Clarke's nucleus (thoracic cord, ~C8–L2); ipsilateral; enters via the inferior cerebellar peduncle

notes.front: Primary motor cortex: gyrus and Brodmann area?
notes.back: Precentral gyrus, area 4

notes.front: DCML fibers decussate as the {{c1::internal arcuate fibers}} in the caudal medulla, then ascend as the medial lemniscus.
Somatotopy of the lateral corticospinal and spinothalamic tracts: {{c1::sacral}} fibers lie most lateral, cervical most medial.
Where is the leg represented on the homunculus, and which artery supplies it?
notes.back: Medial surface (paracentral lobule); ACA

notes.front: Gerstmann syndrome: lesion and tetrad?
notes.back: Dominant angular gyrus: agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia, left-right confusion

notes.front: Broca's aphasia: lesion and features?
notes.back: Dominant inferior frontal gyrus: nonfluent, comprehension intact, repetition impaired

notes.front: Wernicke's aphasia: lesion and features?
notes.back: Dominant posterior superior temporal gyrus: fluent but meaningless, poor comprehension and repetition

notes.front: Klüver-Bucy syndrome: lesion and features?
notes.back: Bilateral amygdala/anterior temporal: hyperorality, hypersexuality, docility

notes.front: Patient H.M.: what was removed and what did he lose?
notes.back: Bilateral medial temporal lobes (hippocampi, 1953); lost ability to form new declarative memories

notes.front: Phineas Gage (1848): what was damaged and what changed?
notes.back: Left frontal lobe (ventromedial prefrontal cortex) by an iron rod; his personality and impulse control changed

notes.front: Fluent speech with intact comprehension but impaired repetition = conduction aphasia from a lesion of the {{c1::arcuate fasciculus}}.
Papez circuit: hippocampus → fornix → {{c1::mammillary bodies}} → anterior thalamic nucleus → cingulate gyrus.
The hippocampal region most vulnerable to hypoxia is {{c1::CA1}}.
What passes through the superior orbital fissure?
notes.back: CN III, IV, V1, VI, plus the superior ophthalmic vein

notes.front: What passes through the internal acoustic meatus?
notes.back: CN VII and VIII

notes.front: What passes through the jugular foramen?
notes.back: CN IX, X, XI and the internal jugular vein

notes.front: Only cranial nerve to exit the dorsal brainstem?
notes.back: CN IV (trochlear); it also fully decussates

notes.front: Trochlear palsy: head posture and when is diplopia worst?
notes.back: Head tilts away from the lesion; vertical diplopia worst looking down and in (stairs, reading)

notes.front: Why does a PComm aneurysm blow the pupil early in CN III palsy?
notes.back: Parasympathetic pupillary fibers run on the outside of the nerve and get compressed first

notes.front: Why is CN VI palsy a 'false localizing sign' in raised ICP?
notes.back: Its long intracranial course over the petrous apex/clivus gets stretched by any rise in pressure

notes.front: Abducens NUCLEUS lesion vs abducens NERVE lesion?
notes.back: Nucleus: ipsilateral horizontal gaze palsy (both eyes). Nerve: only the ipsilateral eye can't abduct

notes.front: UMN vs LMN facial palsy: the key difference?
notes.back: UMN (stroke): contralateral lower face only, forehead spared. LMN (e.g. Bell's): whole ipsilateral face incl. forehead

notes.front: Why does a CN VII lesion cause hyperacusis?
notes.back: Paralysis of the stapedius muscle

notes.front: Taste from the anterior 2/3 of the tongue travels in which nerve?
notes.back: CN VII via the chorda tympani

notes.front: Corneal reflex: afferent and efferent limbs?
notes.back: Afferent V1, efferent VII

notes.front: Pupillary light reflex: afferent and efferent limbs?
notes.back: Afferent II, efferent III (Edinger-Westphal parasympathetics)

notes.front: Jaw jerk reflex: which nerve, and what does a brisk one suggest?
notes.back: V3 for both limbs; brisk = UMN lesion above the pons

notes.front: CN X lesion: which way does the uvula deviate?
notes.back: Away from the lesion

notes.front: LMN CN XII lesion: which way does the tongue deviate?
notes.back: Toward the lesion

notes.front: Which intrinsic laryngeal muscle is NOT supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve?
notes.back: Cricothyroid (external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve)

notes.front: Which cranial nerves run through the cavernous sinus?
notes.back: III, IV, V1, V2, VI (plus the ICA)

notes.front: Argyll Robertson pupil: what is it and the classic cause?
notes.back: Accommodates but doesn't react to light; neurosyphilis

notes.front: What does a relative afferent pupillary defect (Marcus Gunn) indicate?
notes.back: Optic nerve (afferent) lesion on the side that dilates during the swinging flashlight test

notes.front: V2 exits the skull through the foramen {{c1::rotundum}}.
V3 exits the skull through the foramen {{c1::ovale}}.
Diabetic (ischemic) CN III palsy is classically {{c1::pupil-sparing}}, because ischemia hits the core of the nerve.
The {{c1::facial colliculus}} is the bump in the floor of the 4th ventricle made by CN VII fibers looping around the abducens nucleus.
Motor nucleus to the pharynx and larynx (via IX and X): nucleus {{c1::ambiguus}}.
Taste and visceral afferents (VII, IX, X) end in the nucleus {{c1::solitarius}}.
In the cavernous sinus, CN {{c1::VI}} runs free next to the ICA, so it's usually hit first by cavernous lesions.
Bitemporal hemianopia: lesion site and classic cause?
notes.back: Optic chiasm; pituitary adenoma

notes.front: Meyer's loop lesion (temporal lobe): field defect?
notes.back: Contralateral superior quadrantanopia ('pie in the sky')

notes.front: Parietal optic radiation lesion: field defect?
notes.back: Contralateral inferior quadrantanopia

notes.front: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia: lesion and findings?
notes.back: MLF lesion: ipsilateral eye can't adduct on lateral gaze, contralateral eye nystagmus on abduction; convergence intact

notes.front: One-and-a-half syndrome: lesion?
notes.back: PPRF/abducens nucleus plus the ipsilateral MLF

notes.front: Destructive frontal eye field lesion: which way do the eyes deviate?
notes.back: Toward the lesion (a seizure there drives them away)

notes.front: Pontine gaze center (PPRF) lesion: which way do the eyes deviate?
notes.back: Away from the lesion (toward the hemiparesis)

notes.front: Parinaud syndrome: lesion and key findings?
notes.back: Dorsal midbrain (e.g. pineal tumor): upgaze palsy, light-near dissociation, convergence-retraction nystagmus, lid retraction

notes.front: PCA occlusion gives contralateral homonymous hemianopia with {{c1::macular sparing}}, thanks to MCA collaterals at the occipital pole.
Bilateral INO in a young adult strongly suggests {{c1::multiple sclerosis}}.
Disease with mixed UMN + LMN signs and spared sensation?
notes.back: ALS

notes.front: Brown-Séquard: what's lost on which side below the lesion?
notes.back: Ipsilateral: motor + vibration/proprioception. Contralateral: pain/temp (starting 1–2 levels below)

notes.front: A positive Romberg sign points to what kind of ataxia?
notes.back: Sensory (proprioceptive), not cerebellar

notes.front: Syringomyelia: classic deficit and structure damaged?
notes.back: Bilateral cape-like pain/temp loss over shoulders and arms; anterior white commissure

notes.front: Anterior spinal artery infarct: what's spared?
notes.back: Dorsal columns (vibration/proprioception); motor and pain/temp below the lesion are lost

notes.front: Subacute combined degeneration: cause and tracts hit?
notes.back: B12 deficiency; dorsal columns, lateral corticospinal, spinocerebellar tracts

notes.front: Tabes dorsalis: cause and structures damaged?
notes.back: Neurosyphilis; dorsal columns and dorsal roots

notes.front: Central cord syndrome: typical patient and deficit?
notes.back: Older person with cervical spondylosis after hyperextension; arms weaker than legs

notes.front: Conus medullaris vs cauda equina syndrome?
notes.back: Conus: symmetric, early bladder/bowel, mixed UMN/LMN. Cauda equina: asymmetric radicular pain, LMN only, later sphincter loss

notes.front: Syringomyelia is classically associated with a {{c1::Chiari I}} malformation.
In adults the spinal cord ends at about {{c1::L1–L2}}, so lumbar puncture is done at L3–L4 or L4–L5.
Horner syndrome triad?
notes.back: Ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis (ipsilateral)

notes.front: Oculosympathetic chain: the three neurons?
notes.back: Hypothalamus → ciliospinal center (C8–T2) → superior cervical ganglion → along the ICA to the eye

notes.front: Wernicke encephalopathy: triad and cause?
notes.back: Confusion, ophthalmoplegia, ataxia; thiamine (B1) deficiency, mammillary bodies hit

notes.front: Guillain-Barré: pattern and CSF finding?
notes.back: Ascending symmetric weakness with areflexia; albuminocytologic dissociation (high protein, normal cells)

notes.front: Myasthenia gravis vs Lambert-Eaton antibodies?
notes.back: MG: anti-AChR (postsynaptic). LEMS: anti-P/Q-type voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channel (presynaptic)

notes.front: MS lesions perpendicular to the lateral ventricles on MRI are called?
notes.back: Dawson's fingers

notes.front: Trigeminal neuralgia: usual vessel compressing the nerve?
notes.back: Superior cerebellar artery; treated surgically by microvascular decompression

notes.front: Absence seizures show {{c1::3 Hz spike-and-wave}} on EEG and involve thalamic T-type Ca²⁺ channels.
Wallenberg (lateral medullary) syndrome: vessel?
notes.back: Vertebral artery or PICA

notes.front: Wallenberg: the crossed sensory finding?
notes.back: Ipsilateral face pain/temp loss + contralateral body pain/temp loss

notes.front: Medial medullary (Dejerine) syndrome findings?
notes.back: Contralateral hemiparesis and DCML loss + ipsilateral tongue deviation (XII)

notes.front: Weber syndrome?
notes.back: Midbrain: ipsilateral CN III palsy + contralateral hemiparesis (cerebral peduncle)

notes.front: Benedikt syndrome?
notes.back: Midbrain tegmentum: ipsilateral CN III palsy + contralateral tremor/ataxia (red nucleus)

notes.front: Millard-Gubler syndrome?
notes.back: Ventral pons: ipsilateral VI and VII palsy + contralateral hemiparesis

notes.front: Locked-in syndrome: lesion and what's preserved?
notes.back: Ventral pons (often basilar occlusion); consciousness, vertical eye movements and blinking preserved

notes.front: Lateral pontine (AICA) syndrome: what distinguishes it from Wallenberg?
notes.back: Ipsilateral facial paralysis and hearing loss (labyrinthine artery)

notes.front: Brainstem nuclei for norepinephrine and serotonin?
notes.back: NE: locus coeruleus (pons). 5-HT: raphe nuclei

notes.front: In Wallenberg syndrome, dysphagia and hoarseness come from damage to the nucleus {{c1::ambiguus}}.
notes.back: Specific to the PICA/lateral medulla, absent in AICA strokes

notes.front: The vomiting center's chemoreceptor trigger zone sits in the {{c1::area postrema}}, which lacks a blood-brain barrier.
ACA infarct: deficit?
notes.back: Contralateral leg > arm/face weakness and sensory loss

notes.front: MCA infarct: deficit?
notes.back: Contralateral face/arm > leg; aphasia if dominant side, neglect if nondominant

notes.front: Conditions associated with berry aneurysms?
notes.back: ADPKD, Ehlers-Danlos, Marfan, coarctation of the aorta

notes.front: Recurrent artery of Heubner: parent vessel and territory?
notes.back: ACA; head of caudate and anterior limb of internal capsule

notes.front: ACA–MCA watershed infarct: classic deficit?
notes.back: 'Man in a barrel': proximal arm and leg weakness

notes.front: Lacunar infarcts: vessels and mechanism?
notes.back: Lenticulostriate (deep penetrating) arteries; lipohyalinosis from chronic hypertension

notes.front: Pure motor stroke: classic lacune site?
notes.back: Posterior limb of the internal capsule

notes.front: Pure sensory stroke: classic lacune site?
notes.back: VPL of the thalamus

notes.front: Artery of Adamkiewicz: what and where?
notes.back: Largest radicular feeder of the anterior spinal artery, usually left side T9–T12; at risk in aortic surgery

notes.front: Classic SAH presentation and LP finding?
notes.back: Thunderclap 'worst headache of my life'; xanthochromia

notes.front: When does vasospasm peak after aneurysmal SAH?
notes.back: About days 4–14

notes.front: The most common site of a saccular (berry) aneurysm is the {{c1::anterior communicating}} artery.
Thalamic pain syndrome after a VPL stroke is called {{c1::Dejerine-Roussy}} syndrome.
Hypertensive intracerebral hemorrhage most often hits the {{c1::putamen}}.
notes.back: Then thalamus, pons, cerebellum

notes.front: Vertebral arteries join to form the basilar artery at the {{c1::pontomedullary junction}}.
IV thrombolysis for ischemic stroke is given within {{c1::4.5}} hours of last known well.
Selected large-vessel occlusion strokes can get mechanical thrombectomy up to {{c1::24}} hours from last known well (DAWN trial).
In aneurysmal SAH, {{c1::nimodipine}} improves outcomes by reducing delayed cerebral ischemia, not by reliably reversing vasospasm.
Hemiballismus: lesion?
notes.back: Contralateral subthalamic nucleus

notes.front: Direct basal ganglia pathway: dopamine receptor and net effect?
notes.back: D1; excitatory dopamine effect, facilitates movement

notes.front: Indirect pathway: dopamine receptor and net effect?
notes.back: D2; dopamine inhibits it, and its net effect is to inhibit movement

notes.front: Basal ganglia output nuclei?
notes.back: GPi and SNr (GABAergic, inhibit the thalamus)

notes.front: Parkinson disease: neurons lost and inclusion?
notes.back: Dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra pars compacta; Lewy bodies (α-synuclein)

notes.front: Huntington disease: genetics and structure atrophied?
notes.back: CAG repeat in HTT (chromosome 4), autosomal dominant with anticipation; caudate atrophy

notes.front: Main DBS targets for Parkinson disease?
notes.back: Subthalamic nucleus or GPi

notes.front: The subthalamic nucleus is {{c1::glutamatergic}} and excites the GPi.
The DBS target for essential tremor is the {{c1::VIM}} nucleus of the thalamus.
Aqueductal stenosis: which ventricles enlarge?
notes.back: Lateral and third; the fourth stays normal

notes.front: Normal pressure hydrocephalus triad?
notes.back: Urinary incontinence, magnetic gait, dementia ('wet, wobbly, wacky')

notes.front: Chiari I malformation: definition?
notes.back: Cerebellar tonsils herniated ≥5 mm below the foramen magnum

notes.front: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension: classic patient and risk?
notes.back: Young woman with obesity, headache, papilledema, normal imaging; risk of permanent vision loss

notes.front: Lateral ventricles drain to the third ventricle through the {{c1::foramina of Monro}} (interventricular foramina).
CSF is reabsorbed through {{c1::arachnoid granulations}} into the dural venous sinuses.
Only output neurons of the cerebellar cortex, and their transmitter?
notes.back: Purkinje cells; GABA (inhibitory)

notes.front: Where do climbing fibers come from?
notes.back: Inferior olivary nucleus (contralateral)

notes.front: Cerebellar hemisphere lesion: which side are the signs?
notes.back: Ipsilateral limb ataxia; patient falls toward the lesion

notes.front: Cerebellar vermis lesion: classic sign?
notes.back: Truncal ataxia, wide-based gait

notes.front: Dentate nucleus output path?
notes.back: Superior cerebellar peduncle → contralateral VL thalamus (and red nucleus) → motor cortex

notes.front: GABA-A vs GABA-B receptors?
notes.back: GABA-A: ligand-gated Cl⁻ channel. GABA-B: Gi/o GPCR opening K⁺ channels

notes.front: What two things does the NMDA receptor need to open?
notes.back: Depolarization to remove the Mg²⁺ block, plus glycine/D-serine as co-agonist with glutamate

notes.front: Main inhibitory transmitter in the spinal cord and its classic antagonist?
notes.back: Glycine; strychnine

notes.front: Botulinum toxin mechanism?
notes.back: Cleaves SNARE proteins, blocking ACh release at the NMJ

notes.front: Cholinergic nucleus that degenerates in Alzheimer disease?
notes.back: Nucleus basalis of Meynert

notes.front: Which dopamine pathway's D2 blockade causes hyperprolactinemia?
notes.back: Tuberoinfundibular

notes.front: Which dopamine pathway's D2 blockade causes extrapyramidal symptoms?
notes.back: Nigrostriatal

notes.front: Loss of orexin (hypocretin) neurons in the {{c1::lateral hypothalamus}} causes narcolepsy type 1.
Tetanus toxin causes spasm by blocking GABA and glycine release from {{c1::Renshaw cells}} and other inhibitory interneurons.
Rate-limiting enzyme of serotonin synthesis: {{c1::tryptophan hydroxylase}}.
GCS: max score per component?
notes.back: Eyes 4, Verbal 5, Motor 6 (total 3–15)

notes.front: Decorticate vs decerebrate posturing: lesion level?
notes.back: Decorticate (flexion): above the red nucleus. Decerebrate (extension): below it, worse prognosis

notes.front: Cushing triad?
notes.back: Hypertension (wide pulse pressure), bradycardia, irregular respirations; sign of rising ICP

notes.front: Monro-Kellie doctrine?
notes.back: Skull volume is fixed: brain + blood + CSF; a rise in one must be offset by the others or ICP rises

notes.front: Normal adult ICP, and the usual treatment threshold?
notes.back: About 5–15 mmHg; treat above ~22 mmHg (Brain Trauma Foundation)

notes.front: Epidural hematoma: vessel, shape and classic history?
notes.back: Middle meningeal artery (temporal bone fracture); biconvex lens, doesn't cross sutures; lucid interval

notes.front: Subdural hematoma: vessel and shape?
notes.back: Bridging veins; crescent that crosses sutures but not the midline

notes.front: Acute vs chronic subdural on CT?
notes.back: Acute: hyperdense (bright). Chronic: hypodense (dark)

notes.front: Uncal herniation: classic findings?
notes.back: Ipsilateral blown pupil (CN III) + contralateral hemiparesis

notes.front: Subfalcine herniation: what's compressed?
notes.back: Cingulate gyrus under the falx compresses the ACA → contralateral leg weakness

notes.front: Tonsillar herniation: why is it lethal?
notes.back: Compresses the medulla → cardiorespiratory arrest

notes.front: External ventricular drain: what two jobs does it do?
notes.back: Measures ICP and drains CSF

notes.front: Classic EVD entry point and target?
notes.back: Kocher's point (~1 cm in front of the coronal suture, midpupillary line); tip at the foramen of Monro

notes.front: Craniotomy vs decompressive craniectomy?
notes.back: Craniotomy: bone flap is replaced. Craniectomy: flap left off so the swollen brain has room

notes.front: Why does hyperventilation lower ICP, and why only briefly?
notes.back: Low PaCO₂ causes cerebral vasoconstriction; the effect fades and can cause ischemia

notes.front: Neurogenic shock: findings and level?
notes.back: Hypotension with bradycardia from loss of sympathetic tone; cord injury above ~T6

notes.front: A GCS of {{c1::8 or less}} generally means the airway should be secured (intubation).
Cerebral perfusion pressure = {{c1::MAP − ICP}}.
In uncal herniation, ipsilateral hemiparesis (a false localizing sign) comes from the opposite cerebral peduncle being pushed into the tentorium: {{c1::Kernohan's notch}}.
{{c1::Duret hemorrhages}} are midbrain/pontine bleeds from downward herniation tearing basilar perforators.
An EVD transducer is leveled at the {{c1::tragus}} (external auditory meatus), approximating the foramen of Monro.
CSF leaking from the nose is confirmed by detecting {{c1::β2-transferrin}}.
Glioblastoma: classic histology and imaging?
notes.back: Pseudopalisading necrosis; ring-enhancing 'butterfly' lesion crossing the corpus callosum

notes.front: Meningioma: imaging sign and histology?
notes.back: Extra-axial mass with a dural tail; psammoma bodies

notes.front: Most common pediatric brain tumor location, and a classic tumor?
notes.back: Posterior fossa; pilocytic astrocytoma (cystic with mural nodule, Rosenthal fibers)

notes.front: Oligodendroglioma is defined by IDH mutation plus {{c1::1p/19q codeletion}}.
